title: Cosmology
one_line_summary: The closing chapter builds the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker description of a homogeneous, isotropic, expanding Universe, converts it into observable redshift-distance relations (luminosity and angular-diameter distance, the H0 measurement problem, the discovery of acceleration), derives the Friedmann and acceleration equations with a cosmological constant treated as a dark-energy fluid, and then surveys physical cosmology as of mid-2021: thermal history, decoupling and CMB anisotropies, dark matter and structure formation, CMB B-mode polarization as a gravitational-wave detector, nucleosynthesis, inflation and quantum-gravity ideas.
role_in_book: This is the last chapter of the book and acts as a capstone that reuses almost every tool built earlier: the Einstein tensor of a spherically symmetric metric from the stellar-structure chapter becomes the route to the spatial FRW geometry; conserved covariant momenta from the Schwarzschild-orbit chapters give the cosmological redshift; the perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor and its conservation law give the energy equation; the active mass rho + 3p from chapter 8 explains cosmic acceleration; the energy-method treatment of orbits returns as an effective-potential view of R(t); and the gravitational-wave chapters (standard sirens, LISA, transverse area-preserving waves) reappear as tools for H0, dark energy and CMB B-modes. Sections 13.1-13.3 are a compact but genuine GR derivation; section 13.4 shifts into a qualitative, observation-rich survey that closes the book on open problems (Hubble tension, dark matter, dark energy, inflation, quantum gravity).

learning_objectives: Explain, with the M/R estimate, why the Universe as a whole requires general relativity while local physics does not, and why Newtonian gravity cannot give a consistent edge-free cosmology.
State the observational basis for homogeneity, isotropy and uniform expansion, distinguish homogeneity from isotropy, and define the cosmic rest frame via the CMB dipole.
Distinguish the particle horizon from the optical (decoupling) horizon and articulate the cosmological principle and what rests on it.
Derive the FRW line element from comoving coordinates, a common scale factor, g_0i = 0, and a spatially constant curvature scalar, including the normalization of k to +1, 0, -1.
Describe the three spatial geometries (flat, three-sphere, hyperboloid in Minkowski space) and argue why each is homogeneous and isotropic.
Derive 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_e) from conservation of p_chi, show H = Rdot/R, and recover v = z = H_0 d for nearby sources.
Define luminosity and angular-diameter distance operationally, derive d_L = R_0 r (1+z) by photon counting and d_A = d_L/(1+z)^2, and expand both to second order in z.
Explain the distance ladder (parallax, Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae, TRGB), standard sirens, CMB/BAO methods, and the origin of the Hubble tension.
Interpret a magnitude-redshift diagram and explain why curvature of the high-z data, not the low-z slope, reveals acceleration.
Derive the cosmological energy equation, the Friedmann equation with Lambda, and the acceleration equation, and explain why negative pressure can accelerate expansion.
Solve the Friedmann equation for radiation-dominated (R proportional to t^{1/2}) and matter-dominated (t^{2/3}) eras and classify future and past behaviour with the effective-potential picture.
Show that Einstein's static universe needs rho_Lambda = rho_m/2 and is unstable.
Define the critical density and Omega parameters, compute rho_c numerically, and quote the measured Omega_Lambda, Omega_m, Omega_b, Omega_k.
Narrate the thermal history: matter-radiation equality, decoupling, dark ages, Population III stars, reionization, and nucleosynthesis, with order-of-magnitude energies and times.
Explain how CMB polarization separates into E and B modes and why primordial gravitational waves are the only primordial source of B modes.
Explain the horizon and perturbation problems and how exponential inflation driven by vacuum energy addresses both.

teaching_approach.summary: Schutz treats cosmology as the place where every earlier idea pays off. The GR core (13.2-13.3) is short and economical: he borrows the spherically symmetric Einstein tensor from the stellar chapter instead of using symmetry-group machinery, proves homogeneity of each FRW slice with a concrete embedding picture, and keeps kinematics (cosmography) strictly separate from dynamics (Einstein equations). Throughout he forces the reader back to what is actually measured: flux, redshift, angular size. Dynamics are made intuitive by rewriting the Friedmann equation as a particle energy equation and by treating Lambda as a fluid with tension. After that the chapter becomes a narrative survey of physical cosmology, heavily observational and explicitly dated (mid-2021), with gravitational-wave astronomy woven in as a cosmological tool.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: at what scale does M/R approach 1 for uniformly distributed matter, and why can the rest of science ignore this? (local flatness versus Newtonian boundary dependence)
Observed picture: homogeneity, isotropy, uniform expansion, a 2.725 K black-body background, and the headline puzzles (inflation, dark matter, dark energy)
Kinematic description: v = H d, the CMB dipole and cosmic rest frame, the relativity-of-simultaneity objection answered by a preferred but physically defined cosmic time
Assumptions made explicit: particle horizon versus optical horizon, the cosmological principle justified by early observers outside each other's horizons
Model building: comoving coordinates, a single scale factor, g_0i = 0, then a constant 3D curvature scalar forces the FRW spatial metric; normalize k
Check: the three geometries are shown to be genuinely homogeneous and isotropic via Euclidean and Minkowski embeddings
Link to observables: redshift from a conserved momentum, H = Rdot/R, Taylor expansions of R(t), z(t), H(z); Newtonian expanding-cloud cross-check and the fate of photon energy
Cosmography: rebuild distance from flux (photon-counting derivation of d_L), angular-diameter distance, the distance ladder, H0 history and tension, supernova discovery of acceleration

Dynamics: fluid energy equation, one independent Einstein equation, Lambda as dark-energy fluid, the rho + 3p acceleration equation, energy-analogy fates, Big Bang inevitability and its caveats, Einstein's unstable static model
Parametrize our Universe: critical density, Omega sum rule, measured values, baryons versus dark matter, LISA as a future dark-energy probe

Application as thermal history: equality, decoupling, CMB anisotropy map and spectrum, Lambda-CDM, baryon cooling into dark-matter wells, hierarchical mergers and Gaia streams, Population III and reionization
Further applications: evidence for dark matter, CMB plus BAO route to H0, CMB polarization E/B decomposition as a primordial gravitational-wave detector
Back toward t = 0: nucleosynthesis and neutrino counting, pair annihilation and matter-antimatter asymmetry, quark-gluon plasma, then the smoothness and perturbation puzzles resolved by inflation
Frontier: loop quantum gravity, strings and branes; closing reflection that cosmic-scale mysteries may require Planck-scale physics
signature_moves: Recycles the Chapter 10 Einstein-tensor formulas with Phi = 0 to get the curvature of a spherically symmetric 3-space, then imposes constant trace to derive g_rr = 1/(1 - k r^2) in a few lines.

Visualizes k = +1 as a three-sphere in 4D Euclidean space and k = -1 as a constant-interval hyperboloid in Minkowski space, using rotations and boosts respectively to make homogeneity obvious, while warning that the extra dimension is not physical.

Rebuilds v = H d from what is measured: distance enters only as (L/F)^{1/2}, so a luminosity distance is defined and computed by counting photons through a sphere, with one factor of (1+z) from energy and one from arrival rate.
Keeps cosmography (H_0, dH/dt, Taylor series in z) separate from dynamics, so the discovery of acceleration is presented before Einstein's equations explain it.
Treats the cosmological constant as a fluid with rho_Lambda and p_Lambda = -rho_Lambda, then uses the chapter-8 active mass rho + 3p and a rubber-band tension picture to make antigravity plausible.

Rewrites the Friedmann equation as kinetic plus potential energy with -k/2 as total energy, echoing the Schwarzschild effective-potential method, to reason qualitatively about Big Bang, recollapse, and the instability of Einstein's static model.
Repeatedly contrasts with a Newtonian model (boundary-dependent fields, an expanding cloud where redshift is a chain of Doppler shifts) to show what GR adds.
Uses temperature/energy rather than time as the clock for the early Universe, walking backward and forward through energy thresholds.
Integrates gravitational-wave astronomy into cosmology: standard sirens for H_0, LISA for dark energy, B-mode polarization as the CMB acting as a gravitational-wave detector.
Openly time-stamps results (mid-2021) and presents unresolved tensions rather than a closed story.

sections.title: What is cosmology?
sections.summary: Defines cosmology as the study of the Universe as a whole and argues it needs GR: for uniform density M/R grows like R^2, reaching order unity near 6 Gpc, while galaxies (1e-6) and clusters (1e-4) stay Newtonian. Newtonian gravity cannot handle an edgeless uniform medium, whereas GR's local flatness explains why local science can ignore cosmology. The second part lists the observed arena (homogeneity and isotropy above ~10 Mpc, uniform expansion, 2.725 K CMB), notes Olbers' paradox is resolved by finite age, and previews inflation, dark matter and dark energy.
concepts: separation of local physics from cosmology
key_moves: Scale ladder of M/R from Sun to galaxy to cluster to Gpc scales
M = 4 pi rho R^3/3 equals R at about 6 Gpc for rho ~ 1e-26 kg m^-3
Poisson equation needs an outer boundary; GR does not
Converse question: local flatness decouples local experiments from global geometry

sections.title: Cosmological kinematics: observing our expanding Universe
sections.summary: Opens with the observed homogeneity, isotropy (not implied by homogeneity) and uniform expansion, illustrated by the inflating balloon, and the Copernican principle. The Hubble-Lemaitre flow is defined by the local cosmological rest frame, the frame with no CMB dipole; Planck's dipole gives our speed 369.82 km/s. The CMB is expanded in spherical harmonics, anisotropies of ~1e-5 justify homogeneity. H_0 ~ 71 km/s/Mpc is converted to SI and geometrized units and a Hubble time of ~14 Gyr. Objections from simultaneity and v > c beyond 4200 Mpc are answered: v = Hd is local, and a preferred cosmic time exists without violating relativity.
concepts: multipole expansion of the CMB sky
key_moves: Counterexample: uniform magnetic field gives homogeneity without isotropy

Preferred frame is a fact about the contents, not the laws (Jupiter-origin comparison)

sections.title: Models of the Universe: the cosmological principle
sections.summary: Separates two inaccessible regions: beyond our past light cone (bounded by the particle horizon, which grows so cosmology is retrospective) and inside the cone but unobservable (dim objects, events before decoupling behind the optical horizon, which gravitational waves can penetrate). The cosmological principle, or assumption of mediocrity, is motivated by observing two early observers mutually outside their horizons who nonetheless look statistically alike.
key_moves: Past light cone to t = 0 defines what can have influenced us
Early observers with disjoint past cones would have been right to assume mediocrity, so we adopt it too
Optical horizon is not fundamental: gravitational waves cross it

sections.title: Cosmological metrics and the three types of cosmological model
sections.summary: Two idealizations (homogeneous isotropic slices; comoving frame agrees with slicing) lead to comoving coordinates with t as proper time, a single scale factor R(t) multiplying a fixed 3-metric, and g_0i = 0. Isotropy about the origin gives the Chapter 10 form e^{2Lambda}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2; demanding a constant trace of the 3D Einstein tensor and regularity at r = 0 gives 1/(1 - k r^2), hence the FRW metric, with k normalizable to +1, 0, -1. Each case is then checked: flat Euclidean space, a three-sphere (r = sin chi) and a hyperbolic space (r = sinh chi) realized as a Lorentz-invariant hyperboloid in Minkowski spacetime.
concepts: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar

sections.title: Cosmological redshift as a distance measure
sections.summary: Present-day distance to a far galaxy is ill-defined observationally, so redshift is used as a monotonic label. Homogeneity makes p_chi conserved along a radial photon path, giving locally measured energy proportional to 1/R and 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_e), with extra Doppler factors for peculiar motion. Differentiating d_0 = R_0 chi gives v = (Rdot/R)_0 d_0 so H = Rdot/R. The scale factor, redshift, look-back time and H(z) are expanded to second order using H_0 and Hdot_0 (or q_0). A Newtonian expanding cloud reproduces the local picture but depends on its edge; the redshifted photon's energy is simply not conserved in a time-dependent metric, though locally the redshift is a sequence of Doppler shifts.
concepts: redshift as a cosmological distance label
non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology
key_moves: Null radial line: 0 = -dt^2 + R^2 dchi^2; p_chi conserved
Locally measured wavelength scales with R
d_0 = R_0 chi differentiated gives Hubble law with H = Rdot/R
R(t) = R_0 exp(integral of H), Taylor series to second order
Invert z(t) to look-back time, then H(z)
Exact H = -zdot/(1+z)

sections.title: Cosmography: measures of distance in the Universe
sections.summary: Asks how distance entered v = Hd in the first place: through flux of objects of known luminosity. Defines luminosity distance, recalls standard candles and the distance ladder, and notes that standard sirens need inclination because flux up the orbital axis is four times that in the plane. A photon-counting derivation (sphere area 4 pi R_0^2 r^2, photon energy and arrival rate each reduced by 1+z) gives d_L = R_0 r (1+z); the radial null equation relates r to z and yields a second-order expansion. Angular-diameter distance d_A = D/theta = d_L/(1+z)^2 is introduced, with the CMB's intrinsic scale as a key application. The section closes with a methodological moral: physics rests on measurements.

N = L delta t_e / h nu_e photons spread over A = 4 pi R_0^2 r^2
Energy per photon and arrival interval each carry a factor 1+z, so F = L/[A(1+z)^2]
dr/sqrt(1 - k r^2) = dz/(R_0 H(z)); curvature enters only at second order

sections.title: Measuring the Hubble-Lemaitre constant: not a simple matter
sections.summary: Historical sweep from Hubble's ~500 km/s/Mpc through the 50-versus-100 dispute to ~70 by 2000. Explains Cepheids (Leavitt's period-luminosity law, Gaia parallax calibration, possible composition drift), Type Ia supernovae (white dwarf incineration near the Chandrasekhar mass, calibrated by Cepheids in nearby hosts), TRGB and lensing time-delay methods, standard sirens (GW170817 and statistical use of binary black holes, first suggested by Schutz 1986), and early-Universe methods (CMB anisotropies and BAO via angular-diameter distance). States the mid-2021 tension: 74.03 +/- 1.42 from supernovae versus 67.4 +/- 0.5 from the CMB.
concepts: tip of the red giant branch
key_moves: Distance errors, not velocity errors, drove historical H_0 changes
Each rung calibrated on the previous one
Supernova luminosity set by degeneracy physics, largely epoch-independent
Sirens bypass calibration; inclination is the limiting uncertainty
CMB/BAO measure through d_A, supernovae through d_L

sections.title: The Universe is accelerating!
sections.summary: Two supernova teams (High-z, 1998; Supernova Cosmology Project, 1999) extended Type Ia measurements to z ~ 1 and found distant supernovae fainter than expected, best fit by accelerating expansion. The magnitude-redshift diagram (Figure 13.3) is explained: m - M tracks log d_L, the low-z slope gives H_0 and the high-z bending gives acceleration, which cannot be mimicked by rescaling H_0. Omega_M and Omega_Lambda are introduced informally as decelerating and accelerating parameters; the result challenges the belief that gravity always attracts.
key_moves: Dimmer-than-expected at high z means farther than expected, hence faster recent expansion
Residual plot relative to Omega_M = 0.2, Omega_Lambda = 0 isolates the curvature
Acceleration depends on how H changes with z, independent of overall H_0 scale

sections.title: Cosmological dynamics: understanding the expanding Universe
sections.summary: The cosmic contents are a homogeneous perfect fluid at rest in comoving coordinates. The time component of the conservation law gives d(rho R^3) = -p d(R^3): constant rho R^3 for dust and constant rho R^4 for radiation. Isotropy and the Bianchi identity leave one independent Einstein equation, G_tt = 3(Rdot/R)^2 + 3k/R^2, which with Lambda becomes the Friedmann equation; Lambda is recast as dark energy with rho_Lambda = Lambda/8 pi and p_Lambda = -rho_Lambda. The acceleration equation shows rho + 3p drives deceleration, so strong tension accelerates. The energy-equation analogy gives the possible fates; with positive matter and Lambda >= 0 a Big Bang is unavoidable, radiation gives R proportional to t^{1/2}, matter t^{2/3}. Caveats: singularity theorems, quantum effects within a Planck time. Einstein's static model needs rho_Lambda = rho_0/2 and is unstable.
concepts: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
effective potential for the scale factor
key_moves: Isotropy kills spatial components of T^{mu nu}_{;nu} = 0; time component is first law
Only G_tt needed because Bianchi identity links it to G_rr
Move Lambda to the right as T_Lambda = -(Lambda/8 pi) g
Combine energy equation with derivative of Friedmann equation to get Rddot/R = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p)
Kinetic-plus-potential reading: R^2 rho_m falls, R^2 rho_Lambda grows
Solve Rdot^2 = (8/3) pi B R^{-2} to get R^2 proportional to t
Static solution sits at a potential maximum

sections.title: Critical density and the parameters of our Universe
sections.summary: Dividing the Friedmann equation by 4 pi R^2/3 turns every term into an energy density: a Hubble density 3H^2/8 pi, a curvature density -3k/8 pi R^2, matter and Lambda. The Hubble density is the critical density separating open from closed; dividing by it gives Omega_k + Omega_m + Omega_Lambda = 1 with measured values 0, 0.31, 0.69. rho_c = 9.2e-27 h_70^2 kg m^-3; baryons contribute only Omega_b = 0.04, the rest being dark matter. Figure 13.4 summarizes model space and constraints. LISA could measure luminosity distances of high-redshift black-hole mergers, with host identification (possibly aided by Athena) supplying redshifts, to test whether dark energy evolves; weak lensing will limit accuracy.

Threshold logic: physical density below rho_H implies k = -1
Omega sum rule evaluated today

sections.title: Physical cosmology: the evolution of the Universe we observe
sections.summary: Framed as a thermal history using temperature as the clock, reliable back to TeV energies. The decoupling subsection runs backward: dark energy is negligible beyond z ~ 3; radiation (R^{-4}) overtakes matter (R^{-3}) at the equality epoch; decoupling occurs once hydrogen is neutral enough, well below 13.6 eV, releasing the CMB. Dark matter is assumed inert. CMB anisotropies of 1e-5 (Figure 13.5) trace dark-matter density perturbations; slow random velocities are needed for growth, hence cold dark matter and Lambda-CDM. The angular power spectrum (Figure 13.6) carries the parameter information.
concepts: multipole expansion of the CMB sky
key_moves: Scale ratio for equality = Omega_m/Omega_gamma
Decoupling set by residual free electrons, not by the full ionization energy
Positions of spots are random; amplitudes versus l carry physics

sections.title: Dark matter and galaxy formation: the Universe after decoupling
sections.summary: Simulations started from CMB-like perturbations show dark-matter wells growing and neutral baryons falling in after decoupling. Baryons radiate collisional excitation energy, sinking deeper while heating (negative specific heat), whereas collisionless dark matter forms extended halos. Structure builds hierarchically from ~1e6 solar-mass clumps; mergers continue (Omega Centauri, Magellanic Clouds, future Andromeda merger). Gaia's velocity maps preserve formation history because stars conserve phase-space density (Figure 13.7), revealing a major merger ~10 Gyr ago. Population III stars (100-1000 solar masses) enriched the gas, likely left black holes, and reionized hydrogen between z ~ 20 and 8, ending the dark ages; LISA may see black-hole mergers from that era.

galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation
key_moves: Collision time longer than radiative decay time lets photons carry energy out of the well

sections.title: What is the dark matter?
sections.summary: Evidence independent of structure formation: Zwicky's 1933 virial analysis of Coma, Rubin's rotation curves indicating about six times more dark than visible mass, and lensing by cluster halos. Composition is unknown; candidates include undiscovered weakly interacting particles, primordial black holes or other compact objects; laboratory searches so far are negative. A footnote notes Zwicky also proposed neutron stars with Baade in the same period.
key_moves: Virial theorem: velocities too large for luminous mass
Flat rotation curves

sections.title: Using the CMB to measure H_0
sections.summary: The CMB route needs a physical length D to turn angular scales into a distance. The book's version: rather than computing acoustic travel distances directly, one uses BAO. After decoupling, photon drag briefly stops baryons collapsing (decoupling at z = 1090, drag ending at z = 1060), and the imprint of the linear oscillations survives in today's galaxy distribution. Measuring that imprint now and extrapolating back to z = 1060 and then 1090 gives D, hence d_A to last scattering and H_0 = 67.4 +/- 0.5, nearly five sigma from the supernova value. Each method has a weak point: distance-ladder systematics for supernovae, and assumptions about post-decoupling perturbation physics and the sound speed for the CMB. Standard sirens could arbitrate. (The book's description of the CMB H_0 method is non-standard; see gaps.)

sections.title: How a stochastic gravitational wave background affects the CMB
sections.summary: Primordial gravitational waves reach us nearly unaltered, and the CMB can detect them. Because the waves are transverse and area-preserving they create no density or temperature perturbation, but they create velocity patterns that polarize scattered light. Scattering from an anisotropic radiation field (hot spot next to cold spot) produces net linear polarization; acoustic waves produce a curl-free pattern that stays curl-free under superposition. A wave travelling toward us squeezes plasma along one sky axis and stretches along the other, Doppler-heating the inflowing gas so polarization aligns with the stretch axis, frozen in at last scattering; a random background gives a pattern with a curl component, the B mode. Complications: vorticity and obliquely travelling waves give curl-free patterns, and polarized Galactic dust is a foreground.

Scattering polarization perpendicular to the plane of incoming and outgoing directions

sections.title: The early Universe: fundamental physics meets cosmology
sections.summary: Runs the clock back from equality: at roughly 200 s and ~50 keV nuclear reactions equilibrate and light nuclei form, mostly helium-4 with traces of helium-3 and lithium; yields depend on the expansion rate and so on the number of relativistic species, limiting neutrinos to three and bounding primordial gravitational waves; dark matter must be heavier than ~50 keV. At ~1 s and ~500 keV electron-positron pairs are in equilibrium; their annihilation leaves one electron per 1e9 photons, implying a matter-antimatter asymmetry also present for protons at a few hundred MeV. Before 1e-5 s there is a quark-gluon plasma, and colliders test physics to ~10 TeV (Higgs found, no supersymmetry). Two things standard physics does not supply: the initial perturbations and the large-scale smoothness of causally disconnected regions (horizon problem).
key_moves: More massless species means stronger gravity and faster expansion, changing helium and lithium yields
Annihilation bookkeeping reveals asymmetry

sections.title: Inflation
sections.summary: Inflation (Starobinsky, Guth, Linde) posits a temporary large vacuum-energy cosmological constant near 1e-35 s giving exponential expansion with growth time tau = (3/8 pi rho_Lambda)^{1/2}. A small, causally smoothed patch is blown up to contain the observable Universe, explaining homogeneity. Lorentz invariance forces vacuum stress-energy to be proportional to the metric, so vacuum energy acts as Lambda; a high-energy phase transition could release it and later convert it to particles. Exponential growth amplifies quantum fluctuations into classical density perturbations and a gravitational-wave background. The model fits the fluctuation amplitude and spectrum but remains a model until its underlying fields are identified.
concepts: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant
key_moves: H^2 = (8/3) pi rho_Lambda gives Rdot/R = constant
Many e-folds map a tiny smoothed region onto today's horizon
Only Lorentz-invariant symmetric (0,2) tensor is g

sections.title: Beyond general relativity
sections.summary: Inflation stays within classical GR, but quantum gravity is needed eventually. Loop quantum gravity replaces the manifold at the Planck scale with tangled loops and can turn the Big Bang into a bounce. String theory aims to unify all forces in higher dimensions; extra dimensions could be Planck-sized or large, with our Universe a brane on which only gravity leaks off, modifying the inverse-square law below a scale now bounded at about 40 micrometres. Brane collisions, shadow matter and extra gravitational radiation are illustrative model possibilities. Closing theme: the youngest cosmic puzzles (dark matter, dark energy, inflation) may require physics near the Planck scale, 1e16 TeV away from collider energies.
key_moves: Classify ideas as model theories: neither predictions nor idle speculation
Short-range gravity tests as windows on extra dimensions

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Twenty-five exercises covering balloon kinematics, the parsec, Newtonian cosmology's boundary dependence, anisotropic expansion, the FRW derivation steps and the k = -1 hyperboloid, redshift and small-z expansions, the magnitude-redshift relation, Christoffel symbols and fluid conservation, T proportional to 1/R, the acceleration equation, the tension paradox, matter-dominated age 2/(3H_0), Einstein's static model and its instability, negative Lambda histories, a numerical thermal history, the redshift of decoupling, the minimum density of a closed universe, and the epochs where particle physics and quantum gravity limit our knowledge.

concepts.name: cosmology
concepts.definition: The science of the Universe treated as one physical system: its large-scale geometry, contents, expansion history, and the origin of the structures that formed within it.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening paragraph of the chapter presents it as both the backdrop for every smaller structure and a laboratory for physics at energies beyond accelerators.

concepts.name: relativistic regime at cosmological scales
concepts.definition: For matter spread with roughly constant density, enclosed mass grows as R^3 so the compactness M/R (geometrized units) grows as R^2; it must eventually approach 1. With rho ~ 1e-26 kg m^-3 this happens around R ~ 6 Gpc, inside the observable Universe, so GR is unavoidable for cosmology.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with compact objects, where R shrinks at fixed M. A ladder of estimates (Sun, Milky Way with M/R ~ 1e-6, clusters ~ 1e-4) shows nothing below cluster scales needs GR, then the uniform-density estimate crosses unity.

concepts.name: boundary-condition ambiguity of Newtonian cosmology
concepts.definition: Poisson's equation for a uniform infinite medium has no unique solution without a boundary condition at some outer edge; in Newtonian gravity the local field inside a uniform region depends on the shape of the distant boundary, even beyond any horizon, so a consistent edgeless Newtonian cosmology does not exist.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in 13.1 as the reason cosmology became physics only after Einstein, reinforced when the Newtonian expanding cloud is discussed (instantaneous forces make dynamics depend on the edge), and worked out in Exercise 13.3.

concepts.name: separation of local physics from cosmology
aliases: local flatness in a cosmological spacetime
concepts.definition: Because spacetime is locally flat in GR, experiments confined to a small region need no knowledge of the global geometry; stars, planets and black holes can be modelled in asymptotically flat spacetime even though the Universe as a whole is strongly relativistic.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as the converse question (how can biology or stellar astrophysics ignore cosmology?) and answered by contrast with Newtonian theory, where far boundaries influence local fields. Framed as GR explaining why the rest of science does not need GR.

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: Nearly perfect black-body radiation filling space, now at 2.725 K, released when the primordial plasma became neutral and transparent; its small direction-dependent temperature and polarization variations record conditions around decoupling and earlier.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among the basic observed facts in 13.1, then used operationally to define the cosmic rest frame and constant-time slices (13.2), and finally treated physically in 13.4 as the relic of decoupling with anisotropies and polarization.

concepts.name: Olbers' paradox
concepts.definition: The old puzzle that in an infinite, eternal universe uniformly filled with stars every line of sight would end on a star and the sky would be bright; it is resolved because the Universe has a finite age (and expands), so we receive light only from sources near enough for it to have arrived.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned briefly as the oldest cosmological puzzle that expansion and finite age resolve.

concepts.name: homogeneity
concepts.definition: The property that on scales well above about 10 Mpc the Universe, at a given cosmic time, has the same average density and the same statistical properties (galaxy types, clustering, composition, evolutionary stage) everywhere.
concepts.how_introduced: Inferred observationally, taking care that deep observations look back in time: the evolution seen is the same in all directions, which supports homogeneity on constant-time slices.

concepts.name: isotropy
concepts.definition: The property that the averaged Universe looks the same in every direction around every point, with no preferred spatial direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Distinguished from homogeneity by a counterexample (a uniform magnetic field pointing one way everywhere would be homogeneous but anisotropic); conversely inhomogeneity would make most observers see a lumpy, anisotropic sky.

concepts.name: Hubble-Lemaitre law
concepts.definition: On average, galaxies recede at a speed proportional to their proper distance, v = H d. It holds for nearby objects (v much less than c) where v is read from redshift; proportionality to distance keeps a homogeneous distribution homogeneous, so every comoving observer sees the same law.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the third observed regularity, visualized with dots on an inflating balloon, then derived in FRW as the small-distance limit of d_0 = R_0 chi. A footnote records the 2018 IAU renaming.

concepts.name: Hubble-Lemaitre parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional expansion rate H(t) = Rdot/R of the scale factor. Its present value H_0 is about 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1, i.e. about 2.3e-18 s^-1 or 7.7e-27 m^-1 in geometrized units.
concepts.how_introduced: First as the slope of v = H d with unit conversions from astronomers' units; then shown in FRW to equal Rdot/R at any time; later expanded in redshift via H_0 and its derivative.

concepts.name: Hubble time
concepts.definition: The inverse of the present expansion rate, t_H = 1/H_0 (about 4.3e17 s or 14 billion years), setting the order of magnitude of the age of the Universe; the actual age differs because the expansion rate has varied.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed directly after converting H_0 and compared with the 4.54-billion-year age of Earth.

concepts.name: Copernican principle
concepts.definition: The working assumption that we do not occupy a special location; for cosmology, that the expansion is not centred on us and other observers see the same recession pattern.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn from the balloon picture: velocity proportional to separation means any dot sees all others receding the same way.

concepts.name: local cosmological rest frame
concepts.definition: At each event, the local inertial frame in which the CMB temperature shows no dipole (no systematic warmer-ahead, cooler-behind pattern); it moves with the Hubble-Lemaitre flow and differs from the motion of any individual galaxy.
concepts.how_introduced: The naive choice (zero mean velocity of neighbouring galaxies) is rejected because of large-scale galaxy flows; the CMB supplies a clean definition.

concepts.name: CMB dipole
concepts.definition: The l = 1 component of the CMB temperature map, produced by our motion relative to the cosmic rest frame; Planck measures the Solar System barycentre moving at 369.82 +/- 0.11 km/s toward Galactic longitude 264.021 deg, latitude 48.253 deg.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the practical way to find our own cosmic rest frame, after describing COBE, WMAP and Planck mapping.
prerequisites: multipole expansion of the CMB sky

concepts.name: multipole expansion of the CMB sky
aliases: spherical harmonic decomposition of CMB temperature
concepts.definition: Writing the sky temperature as a sum over spherical harmonics Y_lm with coefficients T_lm; the index l labels angular scale (roughly 180 deg / l), the dipole encodes our motion, l >= 2 carries intrinsic anisotropy, and resolution sets the maximum usable l (beyond 2000 for Planck).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented with Galactic coordinates (l, b); a footnote warns not to confuse longitude l with the multipole index. Revisited to explain that phases encode random positions while squared amplitudes give the power spectrum.

concepts.name: preferred cosmic time
concepts.definition: A global time coordinate whose constant-time hypersurfaces are homogeneous and isotropic (equivalently, have uniform CMB temperature) and which equals proper time for observers moving with the Hubble-Lemaitre flow.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as an objection: expansion statements seem to ignore relativity of simultaneity, and v = Hd would exceed c beyond 4200 Mpc. Resolved by locality of v = Hd and by noting a preferred frame reflects the matter content, not the laws.

concepts.name: particle horizon
concepts.definition: The boundary between events that could have sent signals to an observer since the Big Bang and those that could not; drawn as the observer's past light cone extended to t = 0. It grows with time, so formerly unknown regions become observable.
concepts.how_introduced: Figure 13.2 (left) shows the unknown regions outside the cone; the growth of the horizon makes cosmology a retrospective science whose future predictions rely on assumptions.

concepts.name: cosmological principle
concepts.definition: The assumption that the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic everywhere, including beyond our particle horizon, so our observable region is typical.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by imagining two early observers whose past light cones were disjoint: we can see both and find them statistically alike, so their assumption of mediocrity would have been correct, and we adopt it too. Flagged as mathematically very restrictive.

concepts.name: optical horizon
concepts.definition: The limit on electromagnetic observation set by decoupling: earlier than that the ionized plasma was opaque, so no light reaches us from before it. It is not a fundamental horizon because gravitational waves (and neutrinos) passed freely.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the second kind of inaccessible region, inside our past light cone but hidden from instruments.

concepts.name: comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: Spatial coordinates attached to observers at rest in the local cosmological rest frame, each keeping fixed x^i, with time t equal to their proper time; expansion then appears only as time dependence of the spatial metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted as a simplification after stating two idealizations about slicing and the Hubble-Lemaitre flow.

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: The single function of time R(t) multiplying a fixed spatial metric, dl^2 = R^2(t) h_ij dx^i dx^j, so proper distances between all comoving points grow by the same factor; a direction-dependent growth would violate isotropy.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by requiring all h_ij to evolve with a common factor (anisotropic growth would give a matrix-valued Hubble law, Exercise 13.4); normalized to 1 at a reference time.

concepts.name: orthogonality of cosmic time slices
concepts.definition: If simultaneity defined by t = const is to match that of comoving observers, the time basis vector must be orthogonal to the spatial ones, so g_0i = 0, while g_00 = -1 because t is proper time along comoving world lines.
concepts.how_introduced: One-line argument from idealization (ii); Exercise 13.5 connects it to homogeneity as seen by galaxies on fixed x^i.

concepts.name: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar
concepts.definition: Starting from the general isotropic 3-metric e^{2Lambda(r)} dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, homogeneity requires every scalar, in particular the curvature scalar (or the trace of the 3D Einstein tensor, which equals minus half of it), to be position independent; integrating this condition and demanding regularity at r = 0 forces g_rr = 1/(1 - k r^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Uses the Chapter 10 Einstein-tensor components with Phi set to zero rather than a fresh curvature computation; the condition is necessary, and sufficiency is then checked separately for each sign of k.

concepts.name: Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.definition: The spacetime line element ds^2 = -dt^2 + R^2(t)[dr^2/(1 - k r^2) + r^2 dOmega^2], the general form for a spacetime foliated by homogeneous, isotropic spatial slices orthogonal to comoving world lines; R(t) carries all dynamics and k the spatial geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from the scale-factor form and the constant-curvature spatial metric; general proofs are deferred to Weinberg and Schutz (1980b), with case-by-case checks in the text.
prerequisites: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar

concepts.name: curvature parameter k
concepts.definition: The constant in the FRW metric that fixes the sign of spatial curvature; rescaling r and R can set its magnitude to 1, leaving three distinct cases k = +1 (closed), 0 (flat), -1 (open), but no rescaling changes its sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by explicitly rescaling an example with k = -3.

concepts.name: flat FRW model
concepts.definition: The k = 0 case, where each constant-time slice is ordinary Euclidean 3-space with all distances scaled by R(t); homogeneity and isotropy are evident.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by absorbing R(t_0) into a rescaled radial coordinate.

concepts.name: closed FRW model
concepts.definition: The k = +1 case: with r = sin chi each slice is a three-sphere of radius R(t), having finite volume but no boundary; rotations of the embedding 4D Euclidean space carry any point to any other, so it is homogeneous and isotropic.
concepts.how_introduced: Coordinate change dchi^2 = dr^2/(1 - r^2), link to Exercise 6.33, and the remark that the balloon analogy fits this case best; the reader is warned the radial direction into 4D is only a visual aid.

concepts.name: three-sphere
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional set of points at fixed distance a from the origin of 4D Euclidean space, with line element a^2[dchi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2]; the area of spheres about any point first grows, then shrinks to zero at chi = pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 6 as the geometry of closed FRW slices.

concepts.name: open FRW model
concepts.definition: The k = -1 case with slices R^2[dchi^2 + sinh^2 chi dOmega^2]: sphere areas grow faster with proper radius than in flat space, so the slice cannot be embedded in Euclidean space, but it is exactly the hyperboloid of events at fixed timelike interval from an origin of 4D Minkowski spacetime, whose invariance under Lorentz transformations makes it homogeneous and isotropic.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the three-sphere; the Minkowski embedding (Exercise 13.8) is used to prove the symmetry in the same way rotations did for k = +1.

concepts.name: redshift as a cosmological distance label
concepts.definition: Using the measured redshift z, which grows monotonically with separation in an expanding universe, to label how far away (and how far back) a source is, because its present-day distance is not directly observable and the source may no longer exist; peculiar velocities spoil this only for nearby objects.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the ambiguity of 'distance now' for light that travelled for billions of years.

concepts.name: conserved momentum from metric symmetry
concepts.definition: If the metric components do not depend on some coordinate, the covariant component of a geodesic's momentum conjugate to that coordinate stays constant along the geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Section 7.4 to show p_chi is conserved for a radial photon in a homogeneous cosmology.

concepts.name: cosmological redshift
concepts.definition: The increase of photon wavelength in proportion to the scale factor between emission and reception by comoving observers, 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_e); motions of source or observer relative to the cosmic frame multiply in extra Doppler factors. For nearby sources it reduces to an ordinary Doppler shift with z = v.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from conservation of p_chi and the locally measured energy -p^0 proportional to 1/R (Exercise 13.9); Exercise 13.10 shows z = v locally; the Newtonian cloud gives a Doppler interpretation.

concepts.name: deceleration parameter
concepts.definition: The dimensionless measure of how the expansion rate changes, q_0 = -R_0 Rddot_0/Rdot_0^2 = -(1 + Hdot_0/H_0^2); named when gravity was expected to slow expansion (q_0 > 0), it is negative for today's accelerating Universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the traditional replacement for Hdot_0 in the Taylor series of R(t), with the remark that the name is now out of fashion.

concepts.name: look-back time
concepts.definition: The cosmic proper time between emission of light now received with redshift z and its reception, approximately t_0 - t = H_0^{-1}[z - (1/2)(1 - Hdot_0/H_0^2) z^2] for small z.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by inverting the Taylor series for z(t), since emission time is not directly measured.

concepts.name: Newtonian expanding-cloud cosmology
concepts.definition: A uniform Newtonian ball of galaxies started with radial velocities proportional to distance from its centre; far from the edge it expands homogeneously and isotropically and shows redshift as accumulated Doppler shifts between diverging galaxies, but instantaneous gravity makes its dynamics depend on the unseen edge.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as a heuristic cross-check after the redshift derivation, used to explain where photon energy seems to go, and to argue only a relativistic theory (with dynamics determined inside past light cones) makes cosmic dynamics well posed.

concepts.name: non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology
concepts.definition: In a time-dependent metric there is no conserved energy along a photon's geodesic, so the energy a cosmologically redshifted photon loses is not transferred elsewhere; it simply has no conservation law to obey.
concepts.how_introduced: Answer to the natural question of where redshifted energy goes, paired with the Newtonian picture in which successive observers simply move faster away.

concepts.name: cosmography
concepts.definition: Mapping the expansion history of the Universe, via distance measures and the redshift dependence of H, without yet using Einstein's equations to explain it.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a distinct language before dynamics; distances must be defined from observables since coordinate and proper distances are unmeasurable.

concepts.name: luminosity distance
concepts.definition: d_L = (L/4 pi F)^{1/2}: the distance at which a source of known intrinsic luminosity L would produce the observed flux F in static Euclidean space. In an FRW universe d_L = R_0 r (1+z), larger than the present proper transverse size factor R_0 r by 1+z because each photon loses energy and photons arrive spread out in time.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by asking how distance entered v = Hd (through (L/F)^{1/2}); computed by counting photons from a flash crossing a sphere of area 4 pi R_0^2 r^2; expanded to second order in z.

concepts.name: standard candle
concepts.definition: A class of sources whose intrinsic luminosity is known, from theory or from calibration on nearby examples, so that measured flux yields luminosity distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Section 9.6 and illustrated by Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae and the tip of the red giant branch.

concepts.name: cosmic distance ladder
concepts.definition: A chain of distance methods starting from geometric parallax of nearby stars, where each brighter standard candle is calibrated with distances from the previous rung so that it can be used farther away.
concepts.how_introduced: Described generically, then made concrete by the Cepheid-to-supernova calibration and its systematic risks.

concepts.name: standard siren
concepts.definition: A compact binary coalescence whose gravitational waveform directly reveals its luminosity distance without astronomical calibration; because the flux along the orbital axis is four times that in the orbital plane, the inclination must be inferred (from polarization measured by a detector network), and a redshift must come from a host galaxy or statistically.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Sections 9.6 and 12.4: GW170817's H_0, statistical use of binary black holes (Schutz 1986), O4 expectations, and LISA mergers at high redshift as dark-energy probes affected by weak lensing.

concepts.name: angular-diameter distance
concepts.definition: d_A = D/theta, the distance at which an object of known proper transverse size D would subtend the observed angle theta in Euclidean space; in FRW d_A = R_e r = d_L/(1+z)^2, where R_e is the scale factor at emission.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by analogy with luminosity distance; the CMB's intrinsic fluctuation scale and BAO are its key uses for H_0.

concepts.name: Cepheid period-luminosity relation
concepts.definition: The strong correlation between a Cepheid variable's pulsation period and its mean intrinsic luminosity, found by Henrietta Leavitt in 1908 from Magellanic Cloud stars at a common distance; calibrated by parallax (now from Gaia), it anchors the extragalactic distance ladder, though it may drift slightly with chemical composition.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as historically the most trusted candle whose recalibrations explain changes in H_0 estimates.

concepts.name: Type Ia supernova
concepts.definition: The explosion of a white dwarf, usually driven by accretion from a companion, in which nuclear burning ignited near the Chandrasekhar mass incinerates the whole star; since degeneracy physics fixes the progenitor mass, peak luminosities are similar and largely independent of cosmic epoch, making them bright standard candles once calibrated with Cepheids in nearby hosts.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with core-collapse (Type II) supernovae that leave neutron stars or black holes; the calibration chain and the discovery of acceleration follow.

concepts.name: tip of the red giant branch
concepts.definition: A distance indicator based on the maximum luminosity red giants reach, believed to be nearly independent of composition and cosmic time.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among alternative calibrators, alongside lensing time-delay modelling.

concepts.name: Hubble tension
concepts.definition: The mid-2021 disagreement, significant at several standard deviations, between H_0 from the supernova distance ladder (74.03 +/- 1.42 km s^-1 Mpc^-1) and from the CMB with BAO (67.4 +/- 0.5), which may reflect unknown systematics in either method or missing physics.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after reviewing methods; revisited once the CMB/BAO route is explained, identifying each method's weak point and suggesting standard sirens as an independent arbiter.

concepts.name: accelerating expansion of the Universe
concepts.definition: The finding, from Type Ia supernovae out to z ~ 1 (1998-99) and since confirmed by other probes, that the expansion rate is increasing today (Rddot > 0), which requires a dominant component with sufficiently negative pressure, most simply a cosmological constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced cosmographically via Figure 13.3 before dynamics; explained in 13.3 by the acceleration equation and dark energy.

concepts.name: magnitude-redshift diagram
concepts.definition: A plot of distance modulus m - M (proportional to log of luminosity distance) against redshift; the low-z slope fixes H_0 and the bending at z ~ 1 measures acceleration. To first order beyond linear, m - M = 5 log10[z/(10 pc H_0)] + 1.09(1 - q_0) z.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off Figure 13.3 with an explanation of magnitudes; its low-z expansion is assigned as Exercise 13.13.

concepts.name: density parameters Omega
concepts.definition: Ratios of energy densities to the critical density. Evaluated today they obey Omega_k + Omega_m + Omega_Lambda = 1; measurements give Omega_Lambda about 0.69, Omega_m about 0.31 (baryons 0.04, dark matter 0.27) and Omega_k about 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed informally to label Figure 13.3 curves, defined properly from the Friedmann equation in 13.3, and mapped in Figure 13.4.

concepts.name: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
concepts.definition: Idealization of matter and radiation as a homogeneous perfect fluid at rest in comoving coordinates, with rho and p depending only on time; any bulk flow would single out a direction and break isotropy.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken over from the stellar chapters with the stress-energy form of Eq. 4.36.

concepts.name: cosmological energy equation
aliases: first law for the expanding Universe
concepts.definition: The time component of T^{mu nu}_{;nu} = 0 in FRW: d(rho R^3)/dt = -p d(R^3)/dt, equivalently rhodot + 3(rho + p) Rdot/R = 0; energy in a comoving volume changes by the -p dV work done as it expands.
concepts.how_introduced: Spatial components vanish by isotropy; the result is derived via Christoffel symbols in Exercise 13.14 and interpreted thermodynamically.
prerequisites: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents

concepts.name: matter-dominated era
concepts.definition: An epoch, including the recent past, when cold nonrelativistic matter with negligible pressure dominates, so rho R^3 is constant; with Lambda = 0 and negligible curvature R grows as t^{2/3}, giving an age 2/(3H_0) if extrapolated to t = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Special case p = 0 of the energy equation; power law quoted and assigned as Exercise 13.19.

concepts.name: radiation-dominated era
concepts.definition: An early epoch dominated by radiation or ultrarelativistic particles with p = rho/3, so rho R^4 is constant; with curvature and Lambda negligible R grows as t^{1/2}, and a black-body temperature falls as 1/R.
concepts.how_introduced: Special case p = rho/3 of the energy equation; solved explicitly to show a Big Bang at finite past time; temperature scaling in Exercise 13.15.

concepts.name: Friedmann equation
aliases: tt-component of Einstein's equations for FRW
energy equation for the scale factor
concepts.definition: (1/2) Rdot^2 = -k/2 + (4 pi/3) R^2 (rho_m + rho_Lambda), the one independent Einstein equation for an FRW model (built from G_tt = 3(Rdot/R)^2 + 3k/R^2), linking expansion rate, spatial curvature and total energy density; equivalently 3H^2/8 pi = -3k/(8 pi R^2) + rho_m + rho_Lambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Isotropy leaves G_tt and G_rr, and the Bianchi identity relates them, so only G_tt needs computing (Exercise 13.16); Lambda is moved into the source as a fluid.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
concepts.definition: A constant term added to Einstein's equations, G_{mu nu} + Lambda g_{mu nu} = 8 pi T_{mu nu}; it is equivalent to a stress-energy -(Lambda/8 pi) g^{alpha beta}, i.e. a fluid with constant energy density Lambda/8 pi and pressure equal to minus that density.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in the tt field equation, reinterpreted as a contribution to the stress-energy that quantum gravity might one day compute, discussed historically (Einstein's static universe and later disavowal), and reused as the engine of inflation.

concepts.name: dark energy
concepts.definition: The energy component that is not tied to any known matter field and drives accelerating expansion; in its simplest form it is the cosmological-constant fluid with rho_Lambda constant in time and p_Lambda = -rho_Lambda, though it might instead be a field whose density and pressure evolve.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in 13.1 as a relativistic energy with negative pressure, named formally in 13.3 via Eq. 13.54, and discussed as an open problem with LISA as a possible test of time variation.

concepts.name: acceleration equation
concepts.definition: Rddot/R = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p), with rho and p totals including dark energy; the expansion decelerates when rho + 3p > 0 and accelerates when it is negative.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived (Exercise 13.17) from the energy equation and the time derivative of the Friedmann equation, instead of from Christoffel symbols, to answer how positive energy can cause acceleration.

concepts.name: active gravitational mass density rho + 3p
concepts.definition: The combination of energy density and (isotropic) pressure that sources gravitational attraction in GR; for dark energy rho + 3p = -2 rho_Lambda, so it gravitates repulsively.
concepts.how_introduced: Linked back to Exercise 8.20, where rho + 3p was the source of the distant Newtonian field, now controlling cosmic deceleration or acceleration.
prerequisites: pressure as a source of gravity

concepts.name: negative pressure (tension)
concepts.definition: A negative diagonal stress component, i.e. tension, as along a stretched rubber band; it is physically ordinary, but dark energy's tension is isotropic and equal in magnitude to its energy density, and tension does not produce any net local force in a homogeneous medium.
concepts.how_introduced: Defused as unphysical-sounding by the rubber band and the balloon's skin; the paradox that tension pulls inward is resolved in Exercise 13.18 (no net pressure force on a uniform element).

concepts.name: effective potential for the scale factor
concepts.definition: Reading the Friedmann equation as kinetic energy (1/2) Rdot^2 plus a potential -(4 pi/3) R^2 (rho_m + rho_Lambda) equal to a constant total energy -k/2, so qualitative past and future behaviour follows from how R^2 rho scales with R, as with orbits in an effective potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Explicitly compared with the energy method for Schwarzschild orbits; used to classify fates, argue the inevitability of a Big Bang, and show Einstein's static model sits at a potential maximum (Exercises 13.20, 13.21).

concepts.name: fate of the Universe
concepts.definition: For positive matter density and Lambda >= 0: an expanding open model expands forever; a flat model expands forever if Lambda > 0, and with Lambda = 0 slows toward zero rate as R grows; a closed Lambda = 0 model reaches maximum size and recollapses to a Big Crunch; a closed Lambda > 0 model's fate depends on the balance of matter and dark energy. All rely on the cosmological principle.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced directly from the energy form of the Friedmann equation; Figure 13.4 shows the dividing line between expanding forever and recollapse.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: Big Bang
concepts.definition: The state R = 0 reached a finite time in the past in any FRW model with positive matter density and nonnegative Lambda; curvature and tidal forces diverge there and classical GR cannot be extended to earlier times.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued via the energy equation (matter term dominates at small R, so R never turned around) and made explicit by the radiation-dominated solution; robustness discussed via singularity theorems and quantum caveats.

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Theorems showing that, given conditions on the stress-energy (such as positive energy) and the validity of Einstein's equations, a universe like ours must have a past singularity even without homogeneity or isotropy, though they do not determine its nature.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited (Hawking and Ellis 1973) to argue the Big Bang does not hinge on symmetry, followed by the caveats on their assumptions.
concepts.notes: The book overstates the theorems. They prove that past-directed timelike geodesics are incomplete, and only under energy conditions. The cosmological version needs the strong energy condition rho + 3p >= 0, which dark energy and the inflaton violate. So inflation plus dark energy weakens, though does not remove, the case for a generic initial singularity. The book does concede that the theorems assume Einstein's equations without Lambda.

concepts.name: Planck time
concepts.definition: The characteristic time of quantum gravity, t_Pl = sqrt(hbar G/c^5), about 5e-44 s (order 1e-43 s), within which classical conclusions about the Big Bang are unreliable because quantum fluctuations can violate energy positivity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced when questioning the singularity conclusion, referencing the Planck mass of Chapter 11; the practical point is that cosmology can start from about 100 Planck times.
concepts.notes: The book prints G M_Pl/c^2, which has dimensions of length; the time needs c^3.

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: The closed, matter-filled FRW model held static by a cosmological constant with rho_Lambda = rho_m/2 (so rho + 3p = 0); it sits at a maximum of the effective potential, so any small change in density makes it expand or collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Told historically (Einstein introduced Lambda before Hubble's discovery and later disowned it), analysed as an equilibrium of the energy equation and assigned as Exercise 13.20 with a stability test.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: critical density
concepts.definition: The total energy density rho_c = 3H_0^2/8 pi (about 9.2e-27 h_70^2 kg m^-3, a few hydrogen atoms per cubic metre) that makes an FRW universe spatially flat; a larger physical density gives a closed model, a smaller one an open model.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by dividing the Friedmann equation by 4 pi R^2/3 so the expansion itself is assigned a 'Hubble energy density' that must equal curvature plus matter plus Lambda densities.

concepts.name: curvature energy density
concepts.definition: The curvature term in the Friedmann equation expressed as if it were an energy density, rho_k = -3k/(8 pi R^2): positive for open (k = -1) and negative for closed (k = +1) models.
concepts.how_introduced: Part of the energy-density bookkeeping that defines the critical density.

concepts.name: h_70 parametrization
concepts.definition: Writing H_0 as h_70 times 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 so formulas can carry the residual uncertainty in the Hubble-Lemaitre constant explicitly; h_70 is close to 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced just before quoting the numerical critical density, with a warning not to confuse it with gravitational-wave amplitude h.

concepts.name: dark matter
concepts.definition: Matter that emits no light and is detected only gravitationally, making up most of the matter density (Omega_d about 0.27 versus Omega_b about 0.04) and apparently not made of ordinary baryons; it seeded structure formation and forms halos, but its particle nature is unknown.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in 13.1, quantified in 13.3 via Omega_b from nucleosynthesis, placed at the centre of structure formation in 13.4, with its own evidence subsection.

concepts.name: baryonic matter
concepts.definition: Matter made of protons, neutrons and electrons; primordial nucleosynthesis fixes its density at Omega_b about 0.04, far below the total matter density.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to split Omega_m into baryonic and dark components.

concepts.name: thermal history of the Universe
concepts.definition: Describing the early Universe as an expanding plasma of radiation and matter in local thermal equilibrium and labelling its epochs by temperature or typical particle energy E = k_B T, which falls monotonically, rather than by t or R.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted at the start of 13.4 because it ties epochs to the physics that operates at each energy; reliability is capped by collider-tested energies around a TeV.

concepts.name: matter-radiation equality
concepts.definition: The epoch when the radiation energy density, scaling as R^{-4}, fell to equal the matter density, scaling as R^{-3}, marking the switch from radiation- to matter-dominated expansion; its redshift is the ratio of today's matter to radiation densities.
concepts.how_introduced: Estimated in the text from Omega_gamma ~ 1e-5 and Omega_m = 0.3 (scale factor ~3e4 smaller than today, ~1e5 K, ~10 eV, ~3000 years).
concepts.notes: Modern values including neutrinos: z_eq about 3400, T about 9000 K (0.8 eV), t about 50,000 yr; the book's numbers are rough and inconsistent with these.

concepts.name: decoupling
concepts.definition: The epoch when the cooling plasma became mostly neutral hydrogen so photons ceased scattering and streamed freely, forming the CMB; it happened at a temperature well below the 13.6 eV ionization energy (because even a small ionized fraction blocks photons), at z about 1090, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in 13.2 as the optical horizon and with z ~ 1090; developed in 13.4 as the end of thermal equilibrium between light and matter.
concepts.notes: Page 448 says z about 2000 and 4e5 yr, while pages 434 and 454 say z = 1090; the latter is correct.

concepts.name: CMB temperature anisotropies
concepts.definition: Small direction-dependent variations of the CMB temperature, of relative size ~1e-5 (about +/-300 microkelvin range in Planck maps), tracing density perturbations at decoupling; their sky positions are random while their amplitude as a function of angular scale is set by early-Universe physics.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited in 13.2 as confirmation that homogeneity is an excellent approximation; mapped in Figure 13.5 and analysed via the power spectrum in 13.4.
prerequisites: multipole expansion of the CMB sky

concepts.name: CMB angular power spectrum
concepts.definition: The mean squared amplitude of the CMB multipole coefficients as a function of l, showing a first acoustic peak near l ~ 200 and a damped sequence of further peaks whose positions and heights constrain cosmological parameters.
concepts.how_introduced: Figure 13.6 shows Planck's measurement; the text explains phases versus amplitudes of T_lm.
prerequisites: multipole expansion of the CMB sky

concepts.name: cold dark matter and Lambda-CDM
concepts.definition: The standard model in which structure grows from small perturbations in dark matter whose random velocities were negligible (cold) at decoupling, so self-gravity could halt the expansion of overdense regions quickly enough to trap baryons, in a spatially flat Universe now dominated by a cosmological constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by simulations requiring low dark-matter pressure for timely galaxy formation.

concepts.name: radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter wells
concepts.definition: After decoupling, infalling gas atoms collide and are excited, and because the density is low they radiate before the next collision; the photons escape the well, draining energy so the baryons sink deeper and actually heat up (negative specific heat), concentrating at the bottom while collisionless dark matter stays extended.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained step by step, linked to negative specific heat in stellar evolution.
prerequisites: negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems

concepts.name: hierarchical structure formation
concepts.definition: The picture in which roughly million-solar-mass gas clumps condense first and then merge repeatedly, building galaxies from hundreds or more mergers; merging continues today.
concepts.how_introduced: Supported by supercomputer simulations; examples include Omega Centauri as a captured core, the Magellanic Clouds, a Milky Way merger about 10 Gyr ago and the future Andromeda merger.
prerequisites: radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter wells

concepts.name: dark matter halo
concepts.definition: The extended distribution of collisionless dark matter surrounding a galaxy or cluster, much larger than the luminous baryonic concentration.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the concentrated baryons; later cited for lensing evidence.

concepts.name: galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation
concepts.definition: Stars in a galaxy are effectively collisionless, so by Liouville's theorem their phase-space density is conserved; groups formed together remain coherent streams in position-velocity space, and Gaia's 3D velocities reveal them and hence the Galaxy's assembly history.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated with Figure 13.7 and the Gaia-Enceladus merger.

concepts.name: Population III stars
concepts.definition: The first generation of stars, formed from pristine hydrogen and helium; the low opacity of metal-free gas meant they had to be very massive (about 100-1000 solar masses), becoming hot, evolving quickly, enriching the gas with heavy elements through winds, and likely leaving many black holes.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as dense pockets in merging structures collapsed; opacity argument explains their mass.

concepts.name: reionization
concepts.definition: The re-ionization of intergalactic hydrogen, neutral since decoupling, by ultraviolet light from the first hot stars, occurring between redshifts of about 20 and 8.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the epoch when the Universe first looked optically somewhat like today.

concepts.name: cosmic dark ages
concepts.definition: The interval between decoupling and reionization with almost no new light production; light from that time was absorbed during reionization, but the low-frequency CMB and gravitational waves pass through, so LISA may observe black-hole mergers from that era.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed as a blind spot for electromagnetic astronomy and an opportunity for gravitational waves.

concepts.name: evidence for dark matter
concepts.definition: Independent gravitational evidence: Zwicky's 1933 virial analysis of galaxy speeds in the Coma cluster, Rubin and collaborators' galaxy rotation curves (about six times more dark than luminous mass), and gravitational lensing by halos of clusters and interacting galaxies.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in its own subsection to show dark matter is not inferred only from structure formation; candidate compositions (new particles, primordial black holes) listed as unresolved.

concepts.name: baryon acoustic oscillations
concepts.definition: The imprint of early sound waves in the coupled baryon-photon plasma, preserved as a characteristic length in the present galaxy distribution; measured today and extrapolated back to the drag and decoupling epochs, it gives the physical size D that turns CMB angular scales into an angular-diameter distance and hence H_0.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the H_0 methods list, explained after photon drag in 13.4.
concepts.notes: The book says the CMB value of H_0 comes from measuring BAO scales today and extrapolating them back to z = 1060 and 1090. It also calls the acoustic waves waves 'in the dark matter'. Both need correcting. The sound waves travel in the photon-baryon plasma, since collisionless dark matter supports no pressure waves. Planck's H_0 = 67.4 comes from the CMB spectra alone: a Lambda-CDM fit computes the sound horizon at last scattering from early-Universe physics and compares it with the measured acoustic angular scale. Galaxy-survey BAO is an independent standard ruler, often combined with the CMB.

concepts.name: photon drag
concepts.definition: In the book's account, the short period after decoupling when gas in overdense regions, heated by compression, was re-ionized and coupled back to the photons, so baryons could not yet fall into dark-matter wells. The book quotes Planck's decoupling at z = 1090 and the end of effective drag at z = 1060.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to explain why the BAO scale is anchored to a slightly later epoch than decoupling.
concepts.notes: The standard picture is different. The 'drag epoch' is when Compton scattering off the still-numerous photons stops holding the baryons back, which happens slightly after last scattering because photons outnumber baryons about 1e9 to 1. It does not involve re-ionization by compressional heating. Teach the z_drag of about 1060 value, but not the book's mechanism.

concepts.name: CMB polarization from anisotropic scattering
concepts.definition: When electrons scatter radiation, the outgoing polarization is perpendicular to the plane containing incoming and outgoing directions; if the incident radiation is brighter from some directions than others (as between a hot and a cold region) the light scattered toward us acquires net linear polarization.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from a 90-degree scattering argument: isotropic radiation cancels, while a hot spot next to a cold spot leaves a net polarization perpendicular to the line joining them.

concepts.name: E-mode and B-mode polarization
concepts.definition: Split of the CMB polarization pattern into a gradient-like, curl-free part (E) and a curl-like part (B); scalar density perturbations (acoustic waves), even when superposed, produce only E, while gravitational waves produce both, so primordial B modes are a signature of gravitational waves at decoupling.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued with vector-field language on the sky: take the curl to remove acoustic polarization; complications (vorticity, obliquely travelling waves, Galactic dust) noted.

concepts.name: primordial gravitational waves
aliases: stochastic gravitational wave background from the early Universe
concepts.definition: Gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe (for example amplified during inflation) that propagate essentially unaltered except for redshift; they could be seen directly by LISA or Einstein Telescope, or indirectly through CMB B-mode polarization, and their energy density is bounded by nucleosynthesis.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the cleanest probe of the earliest times; area-preserving transverse action means no temperature signal, only polarization.

concepts.name: big bang nucleosynthesis
concepts.definition: Formation of light nuclei, mainly helium-4 with traces of helium-3, lithium and others, in the first few minutes as the plasma cooled through tens of keV; heavier nuclei hardly formed because expansion cooled the plasma too fast. Yields depend on the baryon density and the expansion rate, fixing Omega_b about 0.04.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by running the clock back to about 200 s; stars destroy rather than make these light elements, so present abundances are primordial.

concepts.name: nucleosynthesis bound on relativistic species
concepts.definition: Extra massless species would add energy density, strengthen gravity and speed up the early expansion, changing helium and lithium yields; matching observations limits neutrino families to the three known, forces other relativistic backgrounds (including primordial gravitational waves) to be well below the photon density, and requires dark matter to have been nonrelativistic (mass well above 50 keV).
concepts.how_introduced: Argued qualitatively from reaction-network computations.

concepts.name: electron-positron annihilation and photon-to-baryon ratio
concepts.definition: Around kT ~ 500 keV (t ~ 1 s) electron-positron pairs were continually created and annihilated; as the Universe cooled creation stopped and the pairs annihilated, leaving about one electron per 1e9 photons, a ratio that measures the entropy per particle of the Universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Part of the backward walk in energy.

concepts.name: matter-antimatter asymmetry
concepts.definition: No significant antimatter exists today, so in the early plasma matter must have slightly outnumbered antimatter (about one extra particle per billion photons) for both electrons and protons; the physical cause is an open problem of particle physics.
concepts.how_introduced: Inferred from the leftover electrons after annihilation and the absence of anti-galaxies.

concepts.name: quark-gluon plasma
concepts.definition: The state of matter at times earlier than about 1e-5 s, when temperatures and densities were so high that quarks and gluons behaved as free particles rather than being bound into individual protons and neutrons.
concepts.how_introduced: One step in the energy ladder toward collider-tested physics.

concepts.name: horizon problem
concepts.definition: In standard Big Bang models, regions on opposite sides of our sky were outside each other's particle horizons when, for example, helium was made, yet they show the same abundances and conditions; without a causal smoothing mechanism the uniformity must be put in as an initial condition.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed with the right-hand panel of Figure 13.2 alongside the missing origin of density perturbations, as motivation for inflation.

concepts.name: inflation
concepts.definition: A hypothesized very early phase (near 1e-35 s) dominated by a large temporary vacuum energy acting as a cosmological constant, giving exponential expansion with growth time (3/8 pi rho_Lambda)^{1/2}; it stretches a small, causally smoothed region to encompass the observable Universe and amplifies quantum fluctuations into density perturbations and gravitational waves, after which the vacuum energy converts to particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in 13.1; developed after the horizon and perturbation problems, credited to Starobinsky, Guth and Linde, and classed as a model rather than a theory until its fields are identified.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant

concepts.name: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant
concepts.definition: Since the quantum vacuum must look the same to every inertial observer, its stress-energy tensor must be Lorentz invariant, and the only invariant symmetric (0,2) tensor is the metric; hence any vacuum energy behaves exactly like a cosmological constant with p = -rho.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why attempts to compute Lambda focus on vacuum energy and why a high-energy vacuum phase transition could drive inflation.

concepts.name: inflationary generation of perturbations
concepts.definition: During exponential expansion, microscopic vacuum fluctuations are stretched and amplified into classical perturbations, producing both the density fluctuations seen in the CMB (with the right amplitude and spectrum in calculations) and a background of gravitational waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained with a loose comparison to a nonlinear oscillator pumping up its amplitude.

concepts.name: loop quantum gravity
concepts.definition: An approach that quantizes spacetime geometry directly, replacing the smooth manifold at the Planck scale by a network of nested, tangled loops; in some cosmological applications the Big Bang becomes a bounce from an earlier collapsing phase.
concepts.how_introduced: Surveyed briefly as one route beyond classical GR (Bojowald 2008).

concepts.name: string theory and braneworlds
concepts.definition: An approach unifying all interactions, gravity included, using strings in higher-dimensional spacetime; extra dimensions may be Planck-sized or large, with our Universe a four-dimensional brane on which non-gravitational forces are confined while gravity extends into the bulk, altering the inverse-square law below some scale (experimentally below about 40 micrometres).
concepts.how_introduced: Surveyed with the caution that dramatic scenarios come from deliberately simplified model theories.

concepts.name: shadow matter
concepts.definition: Hypothetical matter on a nearby parallel brane that would interact with our world only through gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned among possible brane-world consequences.

key_equations.name: Multipole expansion of the CMB temperature
key_equations.meaning: Sky temperature decomposed into spherical harmonics; l = 1 terms encode our motion (dipole), higher l the intrinsic anisotropy on angular scales of roughly 180 deg / l.
key_equations.symbols: l, b: Galactic longitude and latitude; ell, m: multipole indices; T_lm: complex coefficients; Y_lm: spherical harmonics

key_equations.name: Hubble-Lemaitre law
key_equations.meaning: Local recession velocity is proportional to distance with a direction-independent constant; exact only for v much less than 1.
key_equations.symbols: v: recession speed; H: Hubble-Lemaitre parameter; d: proper distance

key_equations.name: H_0 in several unit systems and the Hubble time
key_equations.meaning: Conversions using 1 Mpc = 3.1e22 m and division by c; the Hubble time is about 14 Gyr, and v = c at d = c/H_0 = 1.3e26 m = 4200 Mpc.
Line element of a constant-time slice in comoving coordinates at a reference time.
key_equations.symbols: h_ij: spatial metric (unrelated to linearized-theory h)

key_equations.meaning: Isotropic expansion requires every spatial metric component to grow by the same factor; otherwise the Hubble law becomes a matrix (Exercise 13.4).

key_equations.name: Scale-factor form of the spatial metric
key_equations.meaning: All proper distances between comoving points scale with one function R(t), normalized to 1 at t_0; h_ij is now time independent.
