General spacetime extension with g_00 = -1 because t is proper time along comoving world lines.
Requiring constant-t slices to match comoving observers' simultaneity sets g_0i = e_0 . e_i = 0.
Most general 3-metric isotropic about one point, borrowed from the spherical-star form (Eq. 10.5).
key_equations.symbols: Lambda(r): metric function (not the cosmological constant); dOmega^2: unit-sphere line element

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor of the isotropic 3-metric
key_equations.meaning: Obtained from the Chapter 10 components (Eqs. 10.15-10.17) by setting Phi = 0, since a static product metric has the same spatial Einstein tensor.

key_equations.name: Trace of the 3D Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: A scalar that must be the same everywhere on a homogeneous slice; in three dimensions it equals minus half the Ricci scalar.

key_equations.name: Homogeneity condition
key_equations.meaning: Setting the trace equal to a constant kappa gives a first-order ODE for e^{-2Lambda}.
Integrated solution; regularity (local flatness) at r = 0 demands the integration constant A = 0 (Exercise 13.7).

key_equations.name: Homogeneous isotropic 3-metric
key_equations.meaning: The unique spatial metric compatible with a constant curvature scalar and isotropy about the origin, with k = -kappa/3.

key_equations.name: Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric
key_equations.meaning: Line element of every homogeneous isotropic cosmology; R(t) holds the dynamics, k the spatial geometry.
key_equations.symbols: t: cosmic time; r: comoving radial coordinate

key_equations.name: Normalization of k
key_equations.latex: \mathrm{d}s^2 = -\mathrm{d}t^2 + \tilde R^2(t)\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde r^2}{1+\tilde r^2} + \tilde r^2\,\mathrm{d}\Omega^2\right],\quad \tilde r = \sqrt3\,r,\ \tilde R = R/\sqrt3\quad(k=-3\to\tilde k=-1)
key_equations.meaning: Worked rescaling for k = -3 showing any nonzero k can be normalized to magnitude 1 while its sign cannot change. Printed error: the book shows 1 - r~^2 in the denominator, but the substitution gives 1 + r~^2 (k~ = -1), as transcribed here.

key_equations.name: Flat slice
key_equations.meaning: For k = 0 each slice is Euclidean space with a rescaled radius.
Defines proper radial coordinate chi for k = +1 with chi = 0 at r = 0.
Integral of Eq. 13.17.

key_equations.name: Three-sphere slice (k = +1)
key_equations.meaning: Metric of a three-sphere of radius R(t_0): finite volume, no edge.

key_equations.name: Hyperbolic slice (k = -1)
key_equations.meaning: Sphere circumferences grow like sinh chi, faster than in flat space; realized as a constant-interval hyperboloid in Minkowski spacetime (Exercise 13.8).

key_equations.name: Radial null line
key_equations.meaning: Line element restricted to a radial photon path in any of the three geometries; the metric is independent of chi so p_chi is conserved.

key_equations.name: Cosmological redshift
key_equations.meaning: Locally measured photon energy scales as 1/R, so wavelength stretches with the scale factor between emission at t and reception at t_0; peculiar motions add further (1 + z) factors.

key_equations.name: Hubble-Lemaitre parameter as expansion rate
key_equations.meaning: Instantaneous fractional expansion rate at any cosmic time.
Present proper distance to a comoving galaxy at coordinate chi.
Rate of change of proper distance, reproducing v = Hd and identifying H_0 = (Rdot/R)_0.
Formal integral of H = Rdot/R.

key_equations.name: Taylor expansion of the scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Second-order expansion; the Hdot_0 term carries acceleration or deceleration information.

key_equations.name: Deceleration parameter
key_equations.meaning: Dimensionless replacement for Hdot_0; positive for deceleration, negative today.
Redshift of light emitted at t, combining Eqs. 13.22 and 13.26.

key_equations.name: Redshift versus emission time
key_equations.meaning: Taylor expansion of Eq. 13.29 (Exercise 13.11).

key_equations.name: Look-back time
key_equations.meaning: Series inversion giving elapsed proper time to an event of redshift z.
Linear expansion of H used with Eq. 13.31 to express H in terms of z.

key_equations.name: Hubble-Lemaitre parameter versus redshift
key_equations.meaning: First-order redshift dependence of the expansion rate.

key_equations.name: Exact H from redshift drift
key_equations.meaning: Exact inversion of Eq. 13.29, with z regarded as a function of emission time t.

key_equations.name: Euclidean flux law
key_equations.meaning: Luminosity inferred from flux for an isotropic emitter at known distance in flat static space.
key_equations.symbols: L: intrinsic luminosity; F: received energy flux

key_equations.name: Luminosity distance
key_equations.meaning: Operational definition of distance for any source of known luminosity, at any redshift.
Photons emitted in interval delta t_e at frequency nu_e.
Proper area of the sphere of photons when it reaches the observer's comoving radius r at t_0.
Each photon's energy is reduced by the redshift factor.
The burst arrives stretched in time by the same factor.

key_equations.name: Flux in an FRW universe
key_equations.meaning: Two powers of 1+z: one from energy per photon, one from arrival rate.

key_equations.name: Luminosity distance in FRW
key_equations.meaning: Relates the observable d_L to the comoving coordinate of the source and redshift.

key_equations.name: Radial photon equation
key_equations.meaning: Connects source coordinate r to redshift; curvature enters only at second order for small r.

key_equations.name: Second-order luminosity distance-redshift relation
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent to d_L = (z/H_0)[1 + (1 - q_0)z/2]; measuring many d_L, z pairs yields H_0 and Hdot_0 (hence acceleration).

key_equations.name: Angular-diameter distance
key_equations.meaning: Distance inferred from the angle subtended by a known proper transverse size.
key_equations.symbols: D: proper diameter; theta: angular size

key_equations.name: Angular-diameter versus luminosity distance
key_equations.meaning: Transverse size is fixed at emission, when the Universe was smaller by 1+z; Exercise cited as 13.17 in text.
Small-z expansion of d_A; unlike d_L it eventually turns over at high z.

key_equations.name: Cosmological energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Time component of stress-energy conservation: energy in a comoving volume changes by -p dV work.

key_equations.name: Matter domination
key_equations.meaning: Dust (p = 0): energy density falls as R^{-3}.
Energy equation with p = rho/3.

key_equations.name: Radiation domination
key_equations.meaning: Radiation energy density falls as R^{-4}: number dilution plus redshift of each quantum.

key_equations.name: tt component of the FRW Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: The only Einstein-tensor component needed, since isotropy and the Bianchi identity make the rest redundant (Exercise 13.16).
Einstein equation with cosmological constant.

key_equations.name: Cosmological constant as stress-energy
key_equations.meaning: Moving Lambda to the source side reinterprets it as a contribution to the stress-energy tensor.

key_equations.name: Dark energy density and pressure
key_equations.meaning: The cosmological-constant fluid has constant density and equal-magnitude negative pressure.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Energy-like first integral for R(t): kinetic term, constant 'total energy' -k/2, and a potential term; rho_m includes radiation.

key_equations.name: Acceleration equation
key_equations.meaning: Expansion accelerates when total rho + 3p < 0, as for dominant dark energy (Exercise 13.17).
Friedmann equation for radiation (rho = B R^{-4}) with k and Lambda neglected.
Separable ODE for the radiation era.

key_equations.name: Radiation-era solution
key_equations.meaning: R reaches zero a finite time ago; choosing T = 0 puts the Big Bang at t = 0, giving R proportional to t^{1/2}.

key_equations.name: Power-law expansion
key_equations.meaning: Scale-factor growth with Lambda = 0 and negligible curvature (matter case: Exercise 13.19).

key_equations.name: Planck time
key_equations.meaning: Epoch within which quantum gravity undermines classical singularity conclusions. The book prints G M_Pl/c^2, which is the Planck length; c^3 is needed for a time.

key_equations.name: Einstein static universe condition
key_equations.meaning: Static matter-dominated model requires dark-energy density half the matter density; the equilibrium is unstable (Exercise 13.20).
key_equations.symbols: rho_0: matter density of the static model

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation as energy densities
key_equations.meaning: Every term read as an energy density.
Hubble density equals curvature plus physical densities; physical density below rho_H implies k = -1.

key_equations.name: Critical density
key_equations.meaning: Threshold density separating open and closed FRW models today.

key_equations.name: Cosmic sum rule
key_equations.meaning: Friedmann equation today divided by rho_c.

key_equations.name: Measured density parameters
key_equations.meaning: Planck 2018 values: a flat Universe dominated by a positive cosmological constant.
Dimensionless scaling of H_0 (not a wave amplitude).

key_equations.name: Critical density in SI units
key_equations.meaning: Numerical value; about 5 hydrogen-atom masses per cubic metre (own estimate).

key_equations.name: Baryons versus dark matter
key_equations.meaning: Most matter is nonbaryonic dark matter.

key_equations.name: Matter-radiation equality estimate
key_equations.meaning: Equality when rho_gamma proportional to R^{-4} meets rho_m proportional to R^{-3}; book's rough inputs (modern radiation density with neutrinos gives about 1/3400).

key_equations.name: Inflationary expansion law
key_equations.meaning: With vacuum energy dominant, H is constant and R grows exponentially.

key_equations.name: Inflation e-folding time
key_equations.meaning: Growth time of the exponential; the text says 20-30 e-folds, standard estimates require about 60.

key_equations.name: Anisotropic Hubble law
key_equations.meaning: If spatial metric components grew at different rates the Hubble law would involve a matrix not proportional to the identity (Exercise 13.4). The printed equation reads v^i = H^i_j with the position factor x^j omitted (confirmed on the page render).
Redshift between emission and reception times (Exercise 13.9).

key_equations.name: Apparent magnitude
key_equations.meaning: Bolometric apparent magnitude relative to a reference flux F_s = 3e-8 J m^-2 s^-1.

key_equations.name: Absolute magnitude
key_equations.meaning: Apparent magnitude the object would have at 10 pc.

key_equations.name: Redshift-magnitude relation
key_equations.meaning: Astronomers' form of Eq. 13.43, the low-z basis of Figure 13.3 (Exercise 13.13).

key_equations.name: FRW Christoffel symbols
key_equations.meaning: Nonvanishing connection coefficients of the FRW metric (Exercise 13.14). The printed Gamma^theta_{phi phi} lacks the minus sign; the correct value is -sin theta cos theta.

key_equations.name: Divergence of cosmic fluid stress-energy
key_equations.meaning: Setting this to zero and multiplying by R^3 gives Eq. 13.47.

key_equations.name: Dynamical equation with matter and Lambda
key_equations.meaning: Time derivative of the Friedmann equation for dust plus Lambda; vanishing at R = R_0 gives rho_Lambda = rho_0/2 (Exercise 13.20).

key_equations.name: Radiation-era temperature-time relation
key_equations.meaning: Temperature of a flat radiation-dominated universe versus time in geometrized units (Exercise 13.25), used to find when particle physics or quantum gravity limits knowledge.

figures.label: Figure 13.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: As a balloon inflates, every pair of painted dots separates at a rate proportional to their separation, so widely spaced dots recede faster than close ones.
figures.visual_description: Two outline circles side by side. The small left circle contains about nine black dots packed closely. The larger right circle contains roughly the same pattern of dots, now spread farther apart, with four short black arrows pointing outward from its rim (up, down, left, right) to indicate expansion. No axes or labels.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniform scaling of a homogeneous distribution produces a velocity-distance law that looks identical from every dot, so no dot is the centre; best suited to the closed k = +1 geometry.

redesign.idea: A 3D balloon with painted galaxies that the learner inflates; any dot can be chosen as 'home' and the view re-centres on it, drawing recession arrows to all other dots and a live v versus d scatter plot whose slope is Rdot/R.
redesign.interaction: Drag a time slider or play button to change R(t) (choose linear, decelerating, or accelerating histories); click a dot to adopt it as observer; toggle arrows measured along the surface versus straight chords to show why distances must be measured within the space; toggle 'flat sheet' and 'saddle' variants for k = 0 and k = -1.

figures.label: Figure 13.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Left: schematic spacetime diagram of our past back to t = 0, showing regions that have not had time to signal us and a region hidden behind intervening matter. Right: the same history with two early observers whose past light cones do not overlap.
figures.visual_description: Two panels, each a large isosceles triangle standing on a horizontal base labelled t = 0, with its apex a black dot labelled 'Our location' on a horizontal line labelled t = now. Left panel: the regions outside the triangle on both sides are labelled 'Unknown'; an arrow labelled 'Particle horizon' points to the triangle's slanted edge; a dashed horizontal line near the base cuts off a strip labelled 'Unobserved'. Right panel: same outer triangle with 'Unknown' outside; near the base two small separate triangles (one drawn in lighter grey) labelled 'Early observers' sit side by side without overlapping.
figures.what_it_teaches: The particle horizon is our past light cone traced to the Big Bang; decoupling hides part of its interior optically; early observers can be causally disconnected from each other yet both visible to us, which underpins the cosmological principle and poses the horizon problem.

redesign.idea: A conformal-time spacetime diagram of an FRW universe where light rays are 45-degree lines; our past cone, the decoupling slice, and user-placed early observers with their own past cones.
redesign.interaction: Slide 'now' upward to watch the particle horizon swallow previously unknown regions; drag two early observers along the decoupling line and see whether their cones overlap; switch between cosmic time and conformal time axes; toggle an inflationary epoch that extends conformal time below the Big Bang line so the early cones do overlap, resolving the horizon problem visually.

figures.label: Figure 13.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Type Ia supernova distance modulus versus redshift from the High-z team is best fit by an accelerating model; the low-z slope fixes H_0 and the high-z bending shows acceleration.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked panels sharing a logarithmic redshift axis z from about 0.01 to just over 1. Top panel: vertical axis m - M in magnitudes from about 33 to 45; black data points with error bars climb diagonally from lower left to upper right; three nearly overlapping curves are drawn, labelled Omega_M = 0.24, Omega_Lambda = 0.76 (solid), Omega_M = 0.20, Omega_Lambda = 0.00 (dotted) and Omega_M = 1.00, Omega_Lambda = 0.00 (dashed). Bottom panel: residuals Delta(m - M) from -0.5 to +0.5 relative to the Omega_M = 0.20, Omega_Lambda = 0 model, which is a horizontal line at zero; scattered points with large error bars; the accelerating model curve rises to about +0.25 at z near 1 and the Omega_M = 1 model curve falls toward -0.5.
figures.what_it_teaches: Luminosity distance versus redshift is the observable; at z ~ 0.5-1 the supernovae are systematically fainter (farther) than a decelerating model predicts, a curvature effect that cannot be removed by changing H_0.

redesign.idea: Live Hubble diagram: a synthetic supernova sample generated from a hidden true cosmology, overlaid with the model curve computed by numerically integrating d_L(z) for learner-chosen parameters, plus a residual panel.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for H_0, Omega_m and Omega_Lambda (with Omega_k derived); a toggle between linear and log axes; a button that changes only H_0 to show the whole curve shifts vertically without bending; a chi-squared readout and an option to add more high-z points and watch the constraint tighten.

figures.label: Figure 13.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Omega_m-Omega_Lambda plane maps possible cosmologies and their histories and fates; supernova, CMB and cluster constraints intersect near Omega_Lambda = 0.7, Omega_m = 0.3, implying Omega_k = 0 within errors, a conclusion strengthened by Planck.
figures.visual_description: Square plot, horizontal axis Omega_m from 0 to 3, vertical axis Omega_Lambda from about -1.5 to 3, header 'Supernova cosmology project'. A dark grey wedge in the upper left is labelled 'No Big Bang'. A long tilted grey ellipse labelled 'Supernovae' runs diagonally from low Omega_m, low Omega_Lambda up toward Omega_m ~ 1, Omega_Lambda ~ 2. A narrow band labelled 'CMB' lies along a straight diagonal line from (0, 1) downward to the right; the line continues to the lower right with labels 'Closed', 'Flat', 'Open' stacked across it. A near-vertical grey band labelled 'Clusters' sits at Omega_m ~ 0.3. A nearly horizontal curve close to Omega_Lambda = 0 separates 'Expands forever' above from 'recollapses eventually' below. A shaded wedge occupies the bottom-right corner. Legend text lists Knop et al. (2003), Spergel et al. (2003), Allen et al. (2002) in different greys. The three constraint regions overlap in a small patch near (0.3, 0.7).
figures.what_it_teaches: Model space is two-dimensional even for simple FRW models: the flat line Omega_m + Omega_Lambda = 1, the expand-forever boundary and the no-Big-Bang region are distinct; independent probes with differently oriented degeneracies combine to pin down a flat, Lambda-dominated Universe.

redesign.idea: Clickable cosmology atlas: the Omega_m-Omega_Lambda plane with region boundaries computed on the fly, linked to a side panel showing R(t) for the clicked point and its effective-potential curve.
redesign.interaction: Click or drag a marker anywhere in the plane; the side panel plots scale factor versus time (showing bounce, recollapse, coasting or acceleration), the Friedmann potential with the 'energy level' -k/2, and the Hubble-diagram curve; layer toggles add schematic supernova, CMB and cluster likelihood ellipses and their combination.

figures.label: Figure 13.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Planck satellite map of small-scale CMB temperature variations, spanning about plus or minus 300 microkelvin.
figures.visual_description: A full-sky map in an elliptical (Mollweide) projection, rendered in greyscale. The oval is filled with fine-grained mottling of light and dark speckles at many scales, with a few larger darker patches (for example near the centre and right edge). There is no colour bar or axes in the exported image.
figures.what_it_teaches: CMB anisotropies are tiny, random in location, and present on all angular scales; their statistics, not individual spots, encode cosmological physics.
concepts: multipole expansion of the CMB sky

redesign.idea: A rotatable CMB sky sphere synthesized from a chosen angular power spectrum, with band-pass filtering in l and an optional kinematic dipole.
redesign.interaction: Rotate the sphere or switch to Mollweide view; select an l range to see which spot sizes it controls; toggle the observer's velocity to add a dipole of adjustable amplitude and direction and then subtract it; re-roll random phases to show that maps differ while the spectrum stays the same.

figures.label: Figure 13.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Planck angular power spectrum of the CMB temperature fluctuations against multipole index l. The caption blames the large low-l error bars on removing our Galaxy's own microwave emission, and notes that at high l the error bars are smaller than the plotted dots.
figures.visual_description: Line plot with vertical axis D_l^TT in microkelvin squared from 0 to 6000 and horizontal axis 'Multipole l' that is logarithmic from 2 to about 30 and linear beyond, up to 2500. Data points with error bars follow a smooth best-fit curve: flat around 1000 at low l with big error bars, rising steeply to a tall first peak of about 5800 near l ~ 220, then a trough near 1700, a second peak near 2600 at l ~ 540, a third of about 2500 near l ~ 810, and progressively smaller oscillations decaying toward about 100 at l = 2500.
figures.what_it_teaches: The physics of the early Universe (acoustic oscillations, damping) imprints a characteristic series of peaks on the fluctuation power as a function of angular scale; this spectrum is what constrains Omega parameters and H_0.

redesign.idea: Linked spectrum and sky: a simplified acoustic-peak model (peak spacing from sound horizon over angular-diameter distance, damping tail) plotted against real data, with each l band linked to its appearance on a synthetic sky patch.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for baryon fraction, matter density and H_0 in the toy model shift peak positions and relative heights; brushing an l range on the plot highlights spot sizes on a sky patch; an explanatory overlay converts l to angle.

figures.label: Figure 13.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Face-on view of the Galaxy showing strings of stars that formed together and have since spread along different paths, revealing an intertwined network rather than a random stellar distribution.
figures.visual_description: A roughly circular tangle of thousands of thin grey line segments and short curved strands with small dots at their ends, densest toward the middle, with a small empty patch near the centre. Darker and lighter strands of varying length cross in all directions like a ball of yarn; there are no axes or labels in the exported image.
figures.what_it_teaches: Because stars are essentially collisionless they keep a memory of their origin in phase space; Gaia's full 3D velocities expose these streams and hence the merger and star-formation history of the Milky Way.
concepts: galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation

redesign.idea: Toy galactic archaeology: release several star clusters in a rotating galactic potential and watch them shear into streams in position space while remaining compact in energy-angular momentum space.
redesign.interaction: Play and scrub time; switch view between face-on positions and an energy versus angular-momentum plot; add a satellite galaxy merger and see new streams appear; colour stars by birth cluster.

worked_examples.label: Scale where GR becomes necessary
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the radius at which a uniform cosmic density makes M/R of order 1, after checking M/R for the Sun, the Galaxy and clusters.
worked_examples.method: Use M/R ~ 1e-6 for the Galaxy (1e11 stars in about 15 kpc) and ~1e-4 for clusters; then set M = 4 pi rho R^3/3 equal to R (geometrized units) with rho ~ 1e-26 kg m^-3.
worked_examples.key_insight: M/R grows as R^2 at fixed density, so relativity must matter on large enough scales even though every smaller system is Newtonian.
worked_examples.result: R ~ 6 Gpc, well inside the observable Universe (seen to beyond 10 Gpc).

worked_examples.label: Converting the Hubble-Lemaitre constant
worked_examples.problem: Express H_0 = 71 km/s/Mpc in s^-1 and m^-1, find the Hubble time, and find the distance at which v = Hd would reach c.
worked_examples.method: Use 1 Mpc = 3.1e22 m; divide by c for geometrized units; invert for t_H; set Hd = c.
worked_examples.key_insight: The expansion timescale is comparable to the age of the Universe, and a naive global v = Hd breaks down at the Hubble distance, forcing a relativistic reinterpretation.

worked_examples.label: Deriving the homogeneous isotropic 3-metric
worked_examples.problem: Find all spherically symmetric 3-metrics whose curvature scalar is the same at every point and regular at the origin.
worked_examples.method: Take G_ij for e^{2Lambda}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 from the Chapter 10 formulas with Phi = 0, form the trace G = -(1/r^2)[1 - (r e^{-2Lambda})'], set it to a constant kappa, integrate to e^{-2Lambda} = 1 + kappa r^2/3 - A/r, impose g_rr(0) = 1 so A = 0, and define k = -kappa/3.
worked_examples.key_insight: Homogeneity can be imposed through a single scalar condition, and machinery already built for stars delivers the answer without group theory.
worked_examples.result: dl^2 = dr^2/(1 - k r^2) + r^2 dOmega^2, hence the FRW metric (13.14).
concepts: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar

worked_examples.label: Normalizing k by rescaling
worked_examples.problem: Show that a metric with k = -3 is the same model as one with k = -1.
worked_examples.method: Substitute r~ = sqrt(3) r and R~ = R/sqrt(3): R^2 dr^2/(1 + 3r^2) becomes R~^2 dr~^2/(1 + r~^2) and R^2 r^2 dOmega^2 becomes R~^2 r~^2 dOmega^2, i.e. the k = -1 form. (The printed Eq. 13.15 shows 1 - r~^2 in the denominator, which would be k = +1; the plus sign is correct.)
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the sign of k is physical; its magnitude trades off against the normalization of R.

worked_examples.label: Identifying the three spatial geometries
worked_examples.problem: Show each sign of k gives a homogeneous isotropic space and identify it.
worked_examples.method: k = 0: absorb R(t_0) into r. k = +1: substitute r = sin chi to get a three-sphere, symmetric under 4D rotations. k = -1: substitute r = sinh chi and recognize the hyperboloid of fixed timelike interval in Minkowski spacetime, symmetric under Lorentz transformations (Exercise 13.8).
worked_examples.key_insight: Embedding spaces make symmetry manifest: rotations or boosts move any point to any other while preserving the slice.
worked_examples.result: Flat Euclidean, spherical (closed, finite volume) and hyperbolic (open) slices.

worked_examples.label: Cosmological redshift and H = Rdot/R
worked_examples.problem: Relate observed redshift to the scale factor and identify the Hubble-Lemaitre parameter in FRW.
worked_examples.method: Place the observer at the origin; radial null path 0 = -dt^2 + R^2 dchi^2; metric independent of chi so p_chi conserved; locally measured energy -p^0 then scales as 1/R (Exercise 13.9). Then differentiate proper distance d_0 = R_0 chi at fixed chi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Redshift measures how much the Universe expanded while the light travelled, and Hubble's constant is the fractional expansion rate.
worked_examples.result: 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_e); v = (Rdot/R)_0 d_0 so H(t) = Rdot/R; locally z = v (Exercise 13.10).

worked_examples.label: Small-redshift cosmography expansions
worked_examples.problem: Expand the scale factor, redshift, look-back time and H to second order about the present.
worked_examples.method: Write R = R_0 exp(integral of H), Taylor expand; combine with 1 + z = R_0/R to get z(t); invert the series for t_0 - t(z); substitute into H(t) = H_0 + Hdot_0 (t - t_0) to get H(z); note the exact inversion H = -zdot/(1+z).
worked_examples.key_insight: At second order the only new cosmological information is Hdot_0 (or q_0), which is exactly what acceleration measurements target.

worked_examples.label: Luminosity distance by photon counting
worked_examples.problem: Compute the flux received from a source of luminosity L at comoving coordinate r and redshift z, and express d_L.
worked_examples.method: Emit N = L delta t_e/(h nu_e) photons; at reception they cover a sphere of proper area 4 pi R_0^2 r^2; each photon's energy is divided by 1+z and the burst duration multiplied by 1+z; divide energy by area and time; use the radial null equation dr/sqrt(1-kr^2) = dz/(R_0 H) to first order to relate r to z.
worked_examples.key_insight: The two separate (1+z) factors (energy and arrival rate) make d_L exceed the naive distance; the emitted frequency drops out, so the result is general.

worked_examples.label: Energy equation for dust and radiation
worked_examples.problem: Specialize d(rho R^3)/dt = -p d(R^3)/dt to pressureless matter and to radiation.
worked_examples.method: Set p = 0 to get rho R^3 constant; set p = rho/3 and rearrange to get rho R^4 constant.
worked_examples.key_insight: Radiation dilutes faster because each quantum also loses energy to redshift (the pdV work), so radiation dominated early and matter later.
worked_examples.result: rho_matter proportional to R^{-3}; rho_radiation proportional to R^{-4}.

worked_examples.label: Radiation-dominated expansion and the Big Bang
worked_examples.problem: Solve the Friedmann equation for a radiation-dominated universe with k and Lambda negligible.
worked_examples.method: Insert rho = B R^{-4} into the Friedmann equation to get Rdot^2 = (8/3) pi B R^{-2}; separate variables R dR = sqrt(8 pi B/3) dt and integrate.
worked_examples.key_insight: R vanishes at a finite past time, so the Big Bang follows from the matter term dominating at small R; matter domination gives t^{2/3} similarly (Exercise 13.19).
worked_examples.result: R^2 = (32 pi B/3)^{1/2} (t - T); choose T = 0 so R proportional to t^{1/2}.

worked_examples.label: Acceleration equation and the role of pressure
worked_examples.problem: Show how a positive dark-energy density can make Rddot positive.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the Friedmann equation in time and eliminate rhodot with the energy equation (Exercise 13.17, using p_Lambda = -rho_Lambda), giving Rddot/R = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p); for dark energy rho + 3p = -2 rho_Lambda.
worked_examples.key_insight: In GR pressure gravitates; large isotropic tension turns the active mass negative and gravity repulsive.
worked_examples.result: Acceleration whenever rho_Lambda exceeds half the matter density (for dust plus Lambda).

worked_examples.label: Qualitative histories from the energy equation
worked_examples.problem: Without solving, determine which FRW models expand forever, recollapse, or began with R = 0.
worked_examples.method: Treat (1/2)Rdot^2 as kinetic energy, -k/2 as total energy and -(4 pi/3) R^2 (rho_m + rho_Lambda) as potential; track how R^2 rho_m (falls as R^{-1} or R^{-2}) and R^2 rho_Lambda (grows as R^2) behave at large and small R.
worked_examples.key_insight: Signs and scalings alone decide fates: k = -1 never stops, k = +1 with Lambda = 0 turns around, and at small R the matter term always wins so a Big Bang is unavoidable if densities are positive.
worked_examples.result: Classification of fates; Big Bang for rho_m > 0 and Lambda >= 0.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

worked_examples.label: Einstein's static universe
worked_examples.problem: Find the dark-energy density that allows a static matter-filled model and test its stability.
worked_examples.method: With rho_m = rho_0 (R_0/R)^3, differentiate the Friedmann equation to get Rddot = (8/3) pi rho_Lambda R - (4/3) pi rho_0 R_0^3 R^{-2}; set it to zero at R_0; check the second derivative of the potential term (Exercise 13.20).
worked_examples.key_insight: The static solution is a potential maximum, so it is unstable: slightly less matter runs away into acceleration, slightly more into collapse.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

worked_examples.label: Critical density and the Omega sum rule
worked_examples.problem: Rewrite the Friedmann equation in terms of energy densities and evaluate the critical density numerically.
worked_examples.method: Divide Eq. 13.55 by 4 pi R^2/3, name 3H^2/8 pi the Hubble density and -3k/(8 pi R^2) the curvature density, divide by rho_c at the present time; insert H_0 = 70 h_70 km/s/Mpc.
worked_examples.key_insight: Whether space is open or closed is decided by comparing the physical density with a density built from the expansion rate.
worked_examples.result: rho_c = 3H_0^2/8 pi = 9.2e-27 h_70^2 kg m^-3; Omega_k + Omega_m + Omega_Lambda = 1 with measured values 0, 0.31, 0.69.

worked_examples.label: Epoch of matter-radiation equality
worked_examples.problem: Estimate when radiation and matter densities were equal.
worked_examples.method: Radiation scales as R^{-4}, matter as R^{-3}; their ratio today Omega_gamma/Omega_m (~1e-5/0.3) equals R_eq/R_0; scale the present CMB temperature up by the same factor.
worked_examples.key_insight: Different dilution laws make any radiation-matter ratio a clock; redshift and scale factor are interchangeable labels.
worked_examples.result: Book: scale factor ~3e4 smaller, T ~ 1e5 K, ~10 eV, ~3000 yr. Modern inputs including neutrinos give z_eq about 3400, T about 9000 K, t about 50,000 yr (own check).

worked_examples.label: Exponential inflation
worked_examples.problem: Find the expansion law when a vacuum energy density dominates.
worked_examples.method: Drop matter and curvature from the Friedmann equation: H^2 = (8/3) pi rho_Lambda is constant, so Rdot/R = 1/tau_Lambda.
worked_examples.key_insight: A constant energy density that does not dilute gives a constant expansion rate and therefore exponential growth, capable of stretching a tiny smoothed patch to cosmic size.
worked_examples.result: R proportional to exp(t/tau_Lambda), tau_Lambda = (3/(8 pi rho_Lambda))^{1/2}.

worked_examples.label: Standard-siren flux anisotropy
worked_examples.problem: Why must the inclination of a binary be known to get its luminosity distance from gravitational waves?
worked_examples.method: Wave amplitude along the orbital axis is twice that in the orbital plane, so the energy flux, quadratic in amplitude, is four times larger; the emission is not isotropic, so L/4 pi F must use the flux emitted in our direction, inferred from the measured polarization ellipticity.
worked_examples.key_insight: Luminosity distance generalizes to anisotropic emitters only if the directional emission is known; polarization supplies that information.
worked_examples.result: Factor 4 flux contrast; inclination-distance degeneracy limits single-event H_0 precision (as for GW170817).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Dots painted on an inflating balloon
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: Hubble-Lemaitre law and the absence of a centre
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Separation along the surface grows in proportion to separation, so every dot sees others receding with v proportional to d; later noted as especially apt for k = +1 and as an example of a medium under tension.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The balloon's interior and exterior (the third spatial direction) have no counterpart in a real three-sphere; it suggests a centre in the embedding space and a finite size even for flat or open models; galaxies themselves do not expand with the rubber.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Balloon demo with a 'hide embedding' button that flattens the view into what surface-dwellers can measure, reinforcing that only in-surface distances count.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Choosing a Solar System origin at Jupiter's position on a particular date
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A frame adapted to the matter content is a convenience, just as nobody would set Solar System coordinates on a moving planet at an arbitrary date; the laws stay frame independent.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The cosmic frame is not merely convenient but physically defined by the CMB and homogeneity everywhere; the analogy understates that the whole foliation is singled out.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Three-sphere as the surface of a 4D ball; hyperbolic space as a hyperboloid in Minkowski spacetime
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: closed and open FRW spatial geometries
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Rotations of the 4D ball and Lorentz boosts of Minkowski space carry any point of the slice to any other, proving homogeneity and isotropy visually.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The embedding dimension is not physical and nothing can move through it; the hyperboloid picture requires comfort with Minkowski geometry and uses a timelike embedding direction.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 2D analogues: a sphere in 3D and a hyperboloid in 2+1 Minkowski space, with drag-to-rotate and drag-to-boost controls that slide a marked point around while triangles drawn on the surface keep their shape.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: An expanding Newtonian cloud of galaxies where a photon passes ever-faster receding observers
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: cosmological redshift as accumulated Doppler shift
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why redshifted photons seem to lose energy: each successive galaxy is moving away faster relative to the previous frame, so each measures a lower energy.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only valid locally; globally the redshift is a property of the time-dependent geometry, and the Newtonian cloud's dynamics depend on its edge.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Chain-of-observers animation: a photon hops between comoving galaxies, with a small Doppler shift at each hop multiplying to the total 1 + z = R_0/R_e.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Friedmann equation as the energy equation of a particle in a potential
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: effective potential for the scale factor
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Kinetic term (1/2)Rdot^2, total energy -k/2, and potential built from R^2 rho; used to read off fates, inevitability of a Big Bang, and the instability of Einstein's static universe as a potential maximum.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: k is fixed by initial data, not an energy one can add; the 'potential' depends on the equation of state, and the analogy obscures that there is no true conserved energy in cosmology.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball-on-a-hill widget: plot V(R) for chosen matter and Lambda, set the energy line -k/2, and roll a ball to generate R(t) alongside.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Tension in a stretched rubber band (and in the balloon skin)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows negative pressure is familiar physics; what is special about dark energy is that its tension is isotropic and enormous.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A rubber band's tension pulls things together locally, which suggests dark energy should decelerate; the cosmic effect comes instead from tension's contribution to the active gravitational mass, not from any mechanical force (Exercise 13.18).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side: a stretched rubber sheet (local forces cancel in the interior) and a gauge showing rho + 3p going negative as tension increases.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Galaxies and clusters as atoms of the cosmic fluid
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: On cosmological scales, galaxies are small enough to be treated as the particles of a smooth fluid.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Galaxy velocities and clustering are not thermal; large-scale flows exist; the analogy says nothing about dark matter.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Inflation amplifying fluctuations like a pumped nonlinear oscillator
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offered as an intuition for how rapid expansion enlarges tiny quantum fluctuations into classical perturbations.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Loose: the real mechanism is modes being stretched beyond the Hubble radius and freezing, closer to parametric amplification in an expanding background than to a driven nonlinear oscillator.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Mode-stretching animation: wavelengths of quantum ripples grow exponentially while the Hubble radius stays fixed; modes that cross it freeze in amplitude.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The CMB as a gravitational-wave detector
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Primordial gravitational waves passing through the last-scattering plasma leave a polarization record, much as a detector records strain; the wry note that the same waves pass through the CMB antenna now.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only waves with wavelengths comparable to the horizon at decoupling leave a signal; the 'detector' is read statistically via B-mode power, not as a time series.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Stars as a collisionless gas that remembers its past
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: galactic stellar streams and phase-space conservation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Liouville's theorem means stars born together stay together in phase space, so the Galaxy is a ball of strings encoding its history.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Scattering by giant molecular clouds, spiral arms and bars slowly erodes coherence.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Temperature as the clock of the early Universe
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Epochs are labelled by the energy scale of the plasma so that each era is tied to the physics active at that energy (ionization, nuclear binding, pair creation, quark confinement).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Temperature is monotonic only while equilibrium holds and species decouple at different times; after decoupling matter and radiation temperatures differ.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Cosmic thermometer timeline: a log-scale slider in energy that shows t, z, R, the dominant species, and which processes are active.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since all galaxies recede from us, we must be at the centre of the expansion.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A velocity proportional to distance is the same law seen from every comoving point; no location is special.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday explosions have a centre, and we only observe from one place.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Hubble-Lemaitre flow velocity at a location is the velocity of the galaxy there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The flow is the velocity of the local cosmological rest frame; individual galaxies have peculiar velocities (typically under 100 km/s) and large-scale flows, and the frame is defined by the CMB.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A preferred cosmological frame contradicts the principle of relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The laws are still the same in every frame; the matter distribution of our one Universe singles out a convenient frame, as any physical system does.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Special relativity is often summarized as 'no preferred frames'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Galaxies beyond about 4200 Mpc recede faster than light, violating relativity, or v = Hd must hold exactly at all distances.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: v = Hd is a local statement for v much less than c; at large distances velocity is not well defined, and one must use redshift and operational distance measures (superluminal recession of comoving coordinates does not violate local causality).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The law looks like a universal linear formula.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: A universe with a uniform field pointing one way everywhere is homogeneous but anisotropic; isotropy about every point is an independent (stronger) property, though it does imply homogeneity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In everyday uniform media both properties usually hold together.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A closed universe has an edge or boundary, and the fourth dimension of its embedding is physically real.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The three-sphere has finite volume but no edge; the embedding direction is only a visualization device inaccessible to measurement (the book notes braneworlds as a speculative exception).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Finite suggests bounded, and pictures of spheres always show the surrounding space.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The energy lost by redshifted photons must be going into something, since energy is conserved.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Energy conservation along geodesics requires a time-independent metric; FRW depends on time, so there is no conserved photon energy and nothing receives it. Locally the loss matches Doppler shifts between receding observers.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Global energy conservation is deeply ingrained from flat-space physics.
concepts: non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The distance astronomers quote for a distant galaxy is its present separation from us.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Present proper distance is unmeasurable (the object may no longer exist); what is measured are luminosity distance, angular-diameter distance or redshift, which differ from one another by powers of 1+z.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In local astronomy distance is unambiguous.
concepts: redshift as a cosmological distance label

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The apparent acceleration could be an artifact of an error in H_0.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Rescaling H_0 shifts the whole magnitude-redshift curve; acceleration shows up as its bending at z ~ 1, which a change of scale cannot produce.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: H_0 itself is uncertain at the several-percent level.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Positive energy density always attracts, so dark energy with positive density cannot accelerate the expansion.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR the source of acceleration is rho + 3p; dark energy's pressure -rho_Lambda makes this -2 rho_Lambda, so it acts repulsively.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian intuition makes mass density the only source of gravity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Negative pressure is unphysical, or tension should pull the Universe inward and slow it down.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Tension is ordinary (rubber bands); in a homogeneous medium it exerts no net force on any element (Exercise 13.18). Its effect on expansion is purely gravitational, through rho + 3p.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Pressure is pictured as a push on walls, and tension as a pull.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang singularity is an artifact of assuming perfect homogeneity and isotropy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Singularity theorems show a past singularity even without symmetry, given positive energy and classical GR; the real caveats are quantum effects and unknown high-energy physics.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Symmetric collapse models often exaggerate focusing.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The optical horizon at decoupling is a fundamental limit on what we can learn about the early Universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only light is blocked; gravitational waves and neutrinos travelled freely, and CMB polarization can reveal earlier gravitational waves. The particle horizon is the fundamental limit.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian gravity can describe an infinite uniform universe just as well as GR.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Poisson's equation in an unbounded uniform medium needs a boundary condition; results depend on the shape of a distant edge, so there is no consistent edge-free Newtonian cosmology.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian cosmology reproduces the Friedmann equation form in textbook derivations.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Primordial gravitational waves would show up as extra temperature fluctuations in the CMB.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book's argument: gravitational waves are transverse and area preserving, so they do not compress the plasma and leave no density signature at decoupling; instead they create velocity patterns that polarize scattered light, detectable as B modes. (Caveat not in the book: tensor modes do add a small large-angle temperature anisotropy through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect, but it cannot be separated from scalar anisotropy, which is why B modes are the clean signature.)
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Density perturbations produce temperature spots, so any perturbation seems likely to.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Most of the matter in the Universe is in stars and gas.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Baryons contribute Omega_b about 0.04 of the critical density, versus Omega_m about 0.31; most matter is nonbaryonic dark matter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Luminous matter is all we see directly.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Astrophysical 'cooling' of gas falling into dark-matter halos makes the gas colder.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Radiating energy away lets the gas sink deeper, and because self-gravitating systems have negative specific heat it actually gets hotter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In the lab, radiating energy lowers temperature.
concepts: radiative cooling of baryons in dark matter wells

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The cosmological redshift is just a Doppler shift, so z = v/c at all distances.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only nearby does z equal v; in general 1 + z = R_0/R_e, a statement about expansion during transit, and z can exceed 1 without any superluminal velocity in a local frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book itself stresses the local Doppler interpretation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Decoupling happens when the temperature drops to the 13.6 eV ionization energy of hydrogen.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Because photons vastly outnumber baryons and even a small ionized fraction scatters light, decoupling waits until kT is far below 13.6 eV (well under 1 eV).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Matching thermal energy to binding energy is the obvious estimate.

thought_experiments.name: Growing sphere of uniform matter
thought_experiments.setup: Start at the centre of the Sun and keep increasing the radius of a sphere, tracking the enclosed mass and M/R through star, galaxy and cluster scales into a uniformly filled Universe.
thought_experiments.lesson: For uniform density M/R grows as R^2, so GR must become necessary at cosmological radii (~6 Gpc) even though all intermediate systems are Newtonian.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Zoom-out slider from solar to Gpc scales with a live M/R gauge that stays near 1e-6 until homogeneity kicks in and then climbs to 1.

thought_experiments.name: Local experiment revealing a distant boundary (Newtonian)
thought_experiments.setup: In a Newtonian universe of uniform density bounded by a non-spherical edge far beyond our horizon, measure the local gravitational field at the centre.
thought_experiments.lesson: The local field would reveal the edge's shape, an unphysical dependence on unobservable regions that GR avoids through local flatness and causal propagation.
concepts: separation of local physics from cosmology
thought_experiments.app_idea: Draw an arbitrary boundary around a uniform 2D mass distribution and show the computed tidal field at the centre changing as the far boundary is reshaped.

thought_experiments.name: Early observers outside each other's horizons
thought_experiments.setup: Two observers at an early epoch lie inside our past light cone but their own past light cones do not intersect.
thought_experiments.lesson: We see both regions as statistically alike, so the principle that unseen regions resemble seen ones would have been right for them; this supports the cosmological principle and highlights the horizon problem.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Part of the Figure 13.2 redesign: drag observers and see cone overlap.

thought_experiments.name: Surprising news from beyond the horizon
thought_experiments.setup: Suppose tomorrow light arrives from a region previously outside our particle horizon showing it to be very inhomogeneous.
thought_experiments.lesson: Our past would then look specially arranged, raising hard questions; predictions about the future depend on assuming mediocrity.

thought_experiments.name: Counting photons from a distant flash
thought_experiments.setup: A source emits a short burst of photons of one frequency; follow them until they cross the sphere through the observer's comoving position.
thought_experiments.lesson: Area grows with R_0^2 r^2, and energy per photon and arrival rate each drop by 1+z, giving d_L = R_0 r (1+z).
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated photon shell expanding in comoving coordinates while each photon's colour reddens and the spacing between photons stretches; counters show area, energy and rate factors.

thought_experiments.name: Photon crossing an expanding Newtonian cloud
thought_experiments.setup: A photon travels outward through a cloud of galaxies whose outward speeds increase with distance from the centre; each galaxy measures its energy as it passes.
thought_experiments.lesson: Each successive observer recedes faster, so measured energies fall; locally the cosmological redshift is a sequence of Doppler shifts.

thought_experiments.name: Perturbing Einstein's static universe
thought_experiments.setup: Start with the balanced static model (rho_Lambda = rho_m/2) and slightly decrease or increase the matter density.
thought_experiments.lesson: Less matter lets dark energy win and expansion runs away; more matter triggers collapse, so the static model is unstable.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ball balanced on the top of the Friedmann potential hill with a nudge button.

thought_experiments.name: Hot spot next to a cold spot, seen by scattering
thought_experiments.setup: Before last scattering, an electron between a hot and a cold region scatters photons through 90 degrees toward us.
thought_experiments.lesson: More photons arrive from the hot side, so the scattered light has a net linear polarization perpendicular to the line joining the spots, and none at spot centres.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Interactive scattering diagram: move a hot and a cold blob around an electron and see the polarization bar we receive rotate and change length.

thought_experiments.name: Gravitational wave heading toward us through the last-scattering plasma
thought_experiments.setup: A primordial gravitational wave propagating along our line of sight stretches plasma along x and squeezes it along y on the sky.
thought_experiments.lesson: Inflowing gas along y is Doppler-heated, raising scattering intensity with polarization along x; last scattering freezes this, producing polarization patterns with a curl component (B modes) when many random waves add.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Sky-patch simulator: generate polarization maps from random acoustic waves (curl-free) versus random gravitational waves, then apply an E/B decomposition and show that only the gravitational-wave map has B power.

thought_experiments.name: B-mode antenna meets its own source
thought_experiments.setup: A CMB telescope receives microwaves carrying a B-mode imprint.
thought_experiments.lesson: The same primordial gravitational waves that created the imprint are passing through the antenna at the same moment, since both travel at the speed of light along the same path.

historical_notes.event: Hubble discovered the linear velocity-distance relation that Lemaitre had predicted; in 2018 the IAU recommended the name Hubble-Lemaitre law.
historical_notes.significance: Recognizes the theoretical prediction alongside the observation; explains the book's naming (footnote 1).

historical_notes.event: Found that Cepheid variables in the Large Magellanic Cloud have mean brightness correlated with pulsation period.
historical_notes.significance: Created the first reliable extragalactic standard candle and the basis of the distance ladder.

historical_notes.event: Hubble's own estimate of the expansion rate was about 500 km/s/Mpc because his distances were too small by a factor of about 7; values of about 50 and 100 competed until around 1990, converging near 70 by 2000.
historical_notes.significance: Shows that distance calibration, not redshift, dominated H_0 uncertainty.

historical_notes.event: Type Ia supernova surveys to z ~ 1 found the expansion accelerating.
historical_notes.significance: Revived the cosmological constant and established dark energy as dominant.

historical_notes.event: Introduced the cosmological constant to permit a static universe, later calling it his biggest mistake once expansion was discovered.
historical_notes.significance: Ironically, Lambda returned as the simplest explanation of acceleration; the static model is unstable anyway.

historical_notes.event: Singularity theorems (reviewed in Hawking and Ellis 1973) showing a past singularity without symmetry assumptions.
historical_notes.significance: Makes the Big Bang robust within classical GR with positive energy.

historical_notes.event: Applied the virial theorem to the Coma cluster and found far more mass than starlight implies, naming the missing component dark matter.
historical_notes.significance: First evidence for dark matter; a footnote notes Zwicky and Baade proposed neutron stars around the same time.

historical_notes.event: Galaxy rotation-curve measurements implying about six times more dark than visible mass around galaxies.
historical_notes.significance: Made dark matter mainstream; the Vera C. Rubin Observatory honours her.

historical_notes.event: Proposed neutron stars at an American Physical Society meeting.
historical_notes.significance: Footnote linking dark matter's discoverer to compact-object history from Chapter 10.
Supplied a mechanism for homogeneity and for the origin of perturbations.

historical_notes.event: Discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC.
historical_notes.significance: Confirms the standard model to about 10 TeV, bounding the energies where cosmology rests on tested physics.

historical_notes.event: Proposed determining H_0 statistically from gravitational-wave standard sirens without identified counterparts.
historical_notes.significance: Basis for using numerous binary black hole events for cosmography.

historical_notes.event: COBE measured the CMB black-body spectrum and first detected its anisotropies.
Pioneered physical cosmology and predicted the CMB.
historical_notes.significance: Cited as the founder of the field treated in 13.4.

historical_notes.event: Gaia data revealed the Gaia-Enceladus merger about 10 Gyr ago.
historical_notes.significance: Direct evidence of hierarchical assembly of the Milky Way.

applications_and_observations.details: Sun and Milky Way have M/R of about 1e-6, rich clusters about 1e-4; a uniform density of 1e-26 kg m^-3 gives M/R = 1 near 6 Gpc, compared with telescope reach beyond 10 Gpc.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Galaxy: 1e11 stars within ~15 kpc; 1 pc = 3e16 m; R(M/R=1) ~ 6 Gpc

applications_and_observations.topic: Planck measurement of the CMB dipole
applications_and_observations.details: Our barycentric velocity relative to the cosmic rest frame from the l = 1 moments; Planck measured multipoles beyond l = 2000, with anisotropies around 1e-5 K.
A representative H_0 = 71 km/s/Mpc gives 2.3e-18 s^-1, 7.7e-27 m^-1, Hubble time 4.3e17 s (~14 Gyr); Earth is 4.54 Gyr old. Peculiar velocities are typically below 100 km/s.
Direct parallaxes of Galactic Cepheids from Gaia (2018) now calibrate the period-luminosity law; possible composition-dependent drift is a systematic concern.
Supernova luminosities are calibrated with Cepheids in nearby host galaxies and then used to measure H_0 and the expansion history.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: H_0 = 74.03 +/- 1.42 km/s/Mpc (Riess et al. 2019)

applications_and_observations.details: GW170817 gave the first siren H_0 with large errors from inclination; binary black holes without counterparts can be used statistically; O4 was expected to yield 200-300 binaries per year; third-generation detectors and LISA could give the most accurate values.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 200-300 binary black holes per year projected for O4 (mid-2021 expectation)

applications_and_observations.details: Supernova ladder versus CMB (with BAO) values differ by nearly five standard deviations as the text states; explanations range from systematics to new physics.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 74.03 +/- 1.42 vs 67.4 +/- 0.5 km/s/Mpc (about 4.4 sigma combined, own calculation)

applications_and_observations.details: High-z Supernova Search Team and Supernova Cosmology Project measured Type Ia supernovae to z ~ 1; distant ones were fainter than in a decelerating model; best fit in Figure 13.3 has Omega_M = 0.24, Omega_Lambda = 0.76.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Residuals of order +0.2 to +0.3 mag at z ~ 0.5-1 relative to an Omega_M = 0.2 empty-Lambda model

applications_and_observations.details: Supernovae, CMB and cluster studies combine to a flat Lambda-dominated Universe; baryons from nucleosynthesis are a small part of the matter.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Omega_Lambda = 0.69, Omega_m = 0.31, Omega_k = 0, Omega_b = 0.04, Omega_d = 0.27; rho_c = 9.2e-27 h_70^2 kg/m^3

applications_and_observations.details: LISA should measure luminosity distances of high-redshift massive black-hole mergers to a few percent; host galaxies may be identified by disturbed morphology, jets or X-ray changes (possibly with ESA's Athena), enabling H(z) at high redshift and tests of time-varying dark energy; weak lensing of the waves adds distance errors.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Distance errors at the few-percent level (projection)

applications_and_observations.details: From Omega_gamma ~ 1e-5 and Omega_m = 0.3 the text estimates equality at a scale factor ~3e4 times smaller than today.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: T ~ 1e5 K, ~10 eV, ~3000 yr after the Big Bang (modern: z ~ 3400, ~50,000 yr, own note)

applications_and_observations.details: The CMB was released when hydrogen became neutral enough for photons to stream freely; CMB temperature today 2.725 K.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: z = 1090, ~380,000 yr (p. 434); text on p. 448 gives z ~ 2000 and 4e5 yr; decoupling kT below 1 eV

applications_and_observations.topic: Planck CMB maps and power spectrum
applications_and_observations.details: All-sky temperature fluctuation map (Figure 13.5) and angular power spectrum (Figure 13.6) from Planck 2018; low-l errors come from subtracting Galactic emission.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Fluctuation range +/-300 microkelvin; first acoustic peak near l ~ 220 (read from figure)

applications_and_observations.details: Omega Centauri is likely the core of an absorbed dwarf and hosts a massive black hole; the Magellanic Clouds will merge with the Milky Way; Gaia (launched December 2013, ~1e9 stars, ~1.5e8 radial velocities) revealed the Gaia-Enceladus Sausage merger, which thickened the disc; Andromeda will merge with the Galaxy.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Gaia-Enceladus ~10 Gyr ago; Andromeda merger in ~3 Gyr; building-block clumps ~1e6 solar masses

applications_and_observations.details: Metal-free first stars were very massive, short-lived, enriched the gas, likely left many black holes, and reionized hydrogen; LISA may see resulting black-hole mergers at z up to 20.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 100-1000 solar masses; reionization between z ~ 20 and 8; Sun formed at z ~ 0.3-0.4, age ~5 Gyr

applications_and_observations.details: Coma cluster virial analysis, galactic rotation curves, lensing by cluster halos and interacting galaxies; direct laboratory searches so far negative; primordial black holes remain a candidate.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Dark-to-visible mass around galaxies about 6:1

applications_and_observations.topic: CMB plus BAO determination of H_0
applications_and_observations.details: As the book describes it, the BAO length scale measured in today's galaxy distribution is extrapolated back to the drag epoch and then to decoupling. That gives a physical size for the CMB fluctuations, hence the angular-diameter distance to last scattering, hence H_0. In practice Planck's H_0 comes from fitting the CMB spectra with a sound horizon computed in Lambda-CDM, and BAO surveys give a complementary ruler (see gaps_and_pitfalls).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Decoupling z = 1090, drag ends z = 1060; H_0 = 67.4 +/- 0.5 km/s/Mpc

applications_and_observations.details: Multiple CMB experiments (as of mid-2021) seek the small curl component of CMB polarization; polarized emission from magnetically aligned Galactic dust must be mapped and removed.

applications_and_observations.topic: Big Bang nucleosynthesis and neutrino counting
applications_and_observations.details: Light elements formed a few minutes after the Big Bang; yields restrict the number of light neutrino species to three and bound any extra relativistic background, including primordial gravitational waves, to below the photon density.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ~200 s, ~50 keV (book); Omega_gamma ~ 1e-5; dark matter mass > 50 keV

applications_and_observations.topic: Pair annihilation and entropy per baryon
applications_and_observations.details: Electron-positron pairs annihilated after about 1 s (~500 keV), leaving one electron per 1e9 photons; proton-antiproton equilibrium at a few hundred MeV about 10 microseconds after the Big Bang; quark-gluon plasma before 1e-5 s.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Photon-to-electron ratio ~1e9

applications_and_observations.details: The LHC probes about 10 TeV, found the Higgs boson in 2012 but no supersymmetry by mid-2021; the Planck scale lies at about 1e16 TeV.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 10 TeV vs 1e16 TeV

applications_and_observations.details: Inflation is placed near 1e-35 s; the text says 20-30 e-foldings could expand a smoothed patch to the observable Universe.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ~1e-35 s; 20-30 e-folds in text (standard estimates ~60)

applications_and_observations.topic: Short-range tests of the inverse-square law
applications_and_observations.details: Laboratory torsion-balance experiments constrain extra-dimension scales in brane models.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Deviations excluded above about 40 micrometres (Lee et al. 2020)

applications_and_observations.topic: Planck time as the limit of classical cosmology
applications_and_observations.details: Classical conclusions about the Big Bang fail within about a Planck time; models can start reliably from ~100 Planck times.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: t_Pl ~ 1e-43 s

k_B is Boltzmann's constant in 13.4; the text explicitly warns not to confuse them.

notation_and_conventions.convention: h_ij is the time-independent comoving spatial metric; h_70 = H_0/(70 km/s/Mpc).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Neither is related to linearized-theory or gravitational-wave amplitude h; the book says so both times.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Cosmological constant in Eqs. 13.52-13.54; rho_Lambda = Lambda/8 pi.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Earlier in the same section Lambda(r) is the radial metric function of Eq. 13.8, borrowed from Chapter 10.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Proper radial coordinate with r = sin chi (k = +1), r = chi (k = 0), r = sinh chi (k = -1).
Quantities evaluated at the present cosmic time t_0 (H_0, R_0, q_0).
notation_and_conventions.notes: In the static-universe discussion and Exercise 13.20, rho_0 and R_0 refer to the static solution instead.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Overdots denote derivatives with respect to cosmic time t, e.g. Hdot_0; zdot in Eq. 13.33 is the derivative of redshift with respect to emission time.
l and b are Galactic longitude and latitude; ell (script l) and m are spherical-harmonic indices.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Footnote 2 warns against confusing l with ell; the exported text sometimes loses the distinction (e.g. T_lm).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Omega_x = rho_x/rho_c with subscripts m (all matter, sometimes M), b (baryons), d (dark matter), Lambda, k (curvature), gamma (photons).
notation_and_conventions.notes: rho_m in Eq. 13.55 includes radiation; Figure 13.3 uses capital M subscripts.

notation_and_conventions.convention: 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_e) for the cosmological part; motions multiply additional (1 + z_motion) factors.
m = -2.5 log10(F/F_s), M = apparent magnitude at 10 pc; larger magnitude means fainter.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Defined in Exercise 13.13; used in Figure 13.3.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Epochs in 13.4 are labelled by E = k_B T in eV, keV, MeV, TeV.
Uses 'Hubble-Lemaitre' law, parameter, constant and time throughout, and 'Friedmann-Robertson-Walker' (not FLRW).
G_ij and its trace G computed for the 3-metric alone; G = -R/2 in three dimensions.

margin_notes.summary: Footnote 1 (dropped by the export, recovered from the render): many sources call H simply the Hubble constant or parameter; the IAU renamed it the Hubble-Lemaitre constant in 2018 to credit Lemaitre's theoretical contribution.
Footnote 2 (dropped by the export, recovered from the render): do not confuse the Galactic longitude l with the multipole index ell.
Footnote 3: Zwicky's dark-matter suggestion came in the same period as his and Baade's proposal of neutron stars at an American Physical Society meeting, discussed in Chapter 10.
Parenthetical warning that the comoving spatial metric h_ij has nothing to do with the metric perturbation of linearized theory; similarly h_70 is not a wave amplitude.
The chapter is explicitly a mid-2021 snapshot; values of H_0, B-mode searches, O4 projections and dark-matter searches are flagged as time-dependent.
Figure 13.3 caption: the low-z slope determines H_0 while the bending at high z demonstrates acceleration; text explains magnitudes grow as objects get dimmer.
Figure 13.4 caption: supernova, CMB and cluster constraints overlap near Omega_Lambda = 0.7, Omega_m = 0.3, so Omega_k = 0 within errors, reinforced by Planck.
Figure 13.6 caption: large low-l errors arise from removing Galactic microwave emission; at high l error bars are smaller than the plotted points.
Remark that the fourth embedding dimension of the three-sphere is only a visual aid, with a forward pointer to brane ideas in the final subsection as a possible different view.

Methodological aside: translating v = Hd into relativity forced a return to measurable quantities; distance, time, velocity, energy and mass are derived from measurements and their global meaning must be guided by that.

difficulty.notes: The GR derivations (FRW metric, redshift, distances, Friedmann equations) are short and use tools already built, so the mathematics is moderate; the second-order cosmography series and the photon-counting derivation require care. Conceptual load is high: multiple distance definitions, horizons, the meaning of a preferred frame, non-conservation of energy, negative pressure, and a large survey of physical cosmology with many unfamiliar numbers and particle-physics terms. Section 13.4 is readable but qualitative and dated, with several numerical slips, so learners need guidance to separate robust ideas from snapshot values.
