teaching_gems.gem: Estimate M/R for ever-larger uniform spheres to show cosmology must be relativistic, then flip the question: local flatness explains why the rest of science never needs cosmology.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Motivates GR for cosmology with one line of arithmetic and immediately gives learners a deep payoff about the equivalence principle.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Scale-zoom slider with an M/R meter and a 'local lab' inset that stays flat no matter how relativistic the global scale becomes.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the FRW spatial metric by demanding a constant curvature scalar in the already-solved spherical-star metric, with regularity at the centre fixing the last constant.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Avoids Killing vectors and group theory yet feels like a genuine derivation, and it reuses familiar machinery so the new result is anchored.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation panel where each line highlights which Chapter 10 formula it borrows, ending with a plot of g_rr(r) for k = +1, 0, -1 including the singular r = 1 for k = +1 explained by r = sin chi.

teaching_gems.gem: Show the k = -1 space is a Lorentz-invariant hyperboloid in Minkowski spacetime, so boosts play the role of rotations on a sphere.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts an unpicturable geometry into special relativity the learner already owns, and proves homogeneity visually.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 2+1D Minkowski viewer with a hyperboloid; a rapidity slider boosts the picture and slides a marked point across the surface while local triangle shapes stay invariant.

teaching_gems.gem: Ask how distance got into v = Hd at all, answer 'through flux', and define luminosity distance, then count photons to get two separate factors of 1+z.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Models the core epistemology of relativity (define quantities by measurement) and makes the (1+z)^2 in the flux memorable as energy loss plus time dilation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Photon-shell animation with three meters (area, energy per photon, arrival rate) whose product updates the flux and d_L as the learner changes z.

teaching_gems.gem: Read the Friedmann equation as a particle energy equation with -k/2 as total energy and R^2 rho as a potential.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Transfers intuition from orbits to cosmology; fates, the inevitability of the Big Bang, and the instability of Einstein's static model all become visual.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Potential-well playground linked to R(t): adjust Omega_m, Omega_Lambda and radiation, set k, and watch the ball-on-hill and the scale-factor history move together.

teaching_gems.gem: Explain cosmic acceleration with active mass rho + 3p and the everyday fact that tension is negative pressure (rubber band, balloon skin).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves 'how can positive energy repel?' without new physics and ties back to an earlier exercise, while Exercise 13.18 blocks the wrong mechanical picture.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Equation-of-state dial w from 1/3 to -1 with live readout of rho + 3p, sign of Rddot, and a small universe animation that decelerates or accelerates.

teaching_gems.gem: Divide the Friedmann equation so that expansion, curvature, matter and Lambda all appear as energy densities; the Hubble density is the critical density.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes Omega bookkeeping and the flatness criterion intuitive as a budget that must balance.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stacked-bar 'cosmic budget' that must sum to rho_H; dragging matter or Lambda bars automatically changes the curvature bar and the geometry icon (sphere, plane, saddle), with a time slider showing how the budget shares evolve.

teaching_gems.gem: Separate CMB polarization into a curl-free part from acoustic waves and a curl part that only gravitational waves can make; note waves are area-preserving so they give no temperature spots.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Uses a vector-calculus distinction learners already know to explain why B modes are a clean gravitational-wave signature.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Polarization sky-patch lab: superpose random plane acoustic waves or random gravitational waves, display headless polarization sticks, and compute E and B maps side by side.

teaching_gems.gem: Use temperature as the clock and walk backward and forward through energy thresholds (ionization, nuclear, pair creation, QCD, collider frontier).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Ties each cosmic epoch to a physical process with a known energy, making the timeline explanatory rather than a list of dates.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Log-energy timeline scrubber showing T, t, z, dominant component, and active process cards (BBN, annihilation, decoupling, reionization).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Planck time is printed as t_Pl = G M_Pl/c^2, which has dimensions of length; the time is G M_Pl/c^3 = sqrt(hbar G/c^5) ~ 5e-44 s.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Dimensional-analysis-minded learners will be confused, or will propagate the wrong formula.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give both Planck length and Planck time with a units check.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise cross-references in the text do not match the exercise list: the energy equation is attributed to Exercise 13.24 (it is 13.14), angular-diameter distance to Exercise 13.17 (13.17 is the acceleration equation; no d_A exercise exists), and the tension discussion to Exercise 13.25 (it is 13.18). Exercise 13.22(c) cites Eq. 12.2, apparently meaning the Friedmann equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students following pointers land on unrelated problems.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected mapping in any course material and add a d_A derivation exercise.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Nucleosynthesis is placed at ~50 keV described as the neutron-proton mass difference; that difference is 1.29 MeV. Weak-interaction freeze-out is near 0.8 MeV, and deuterium-bottleneck nucleosynthesis near 60-80 keV at about 3 minutes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mixes two distinct thresholds and plants an incorrect particle-physics number.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Separate neutron-to-proton freeze-out, free neutron decay, and the deuterium bottleneck on a timeline.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Matter-radiation equality numbers (Omega_gamma ~ 1e-5, scale factor 3e4 smaller, 1e5 K, 10 eV, 3000 years) are off; with photons plus neutrinos z_eq is about 3400, T about 9000 K (0.8 eV), t about 50,000 yr. The text's argument that the equality energy lies near 13.6 eV therefore does not hold numerically.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Wrong epoch ordering intuition and inconsistent numbers relative to decoupling.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Recompute with Omega_r h^2 ~ 4.2e-5 and emphasize that equality precedes decoupling by a factor ~3 in redshift.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Decoupling redshift is given as about 2000 (and 'a little below 1 eV') on one page, but z = 1090 elsewhere; actual decoupling temperature is ~0.26 eV (3000 K).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflicting numbers in the same chapter undermine confidence.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Standardize on z = 1090, T = 3000 K, t = 380,000 yr and explain the photon-to-baryon ratio reason for the low temperature.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Inflation is said to need 20-30 e-foldings; standard estimates require roughly 50-60 to solve the horizon and flatness problems.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Underestimates the enormity of inflation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the e-fold estimate from the ratio of today's Hubble radius to the pre-inflation causal patch.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The statement that our Universe is 'near' Einstein's static solution because dark energy is about twice matter is misleading: static needs rho_Lambda = rho_m/2, ours has about 2.2 rho_m, a factor of about 4 difference, and ours is accelerating (q_0 ~ -0.5).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Could suggest our Universe is nearly static or nearly balanced.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Compute q_0 = Omega_m/2 - Omega_Lambda for both cases.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 13.15, the worked rescaling of k = -3, prints the radial term as dr~^2/(1 - r~^2); substituting r~ = sqrt(3) r into 1 - kr^2 = 1 + 3r^2 gives dr~^2/(1 + r~^2), the k = -1 form. The printed sign contradicts the very next sentence that the sign of k cannot change. Separately, Exercise 13.4's Eq. 13.67 is printed as v^i = H^i_j without the position x^j.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful learner checking the algebra finds the sign flips, which seems to contradict the claim being illustrated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the corrected substitution step by step and make the invariance of sign(k) explicit: rescaling multiplies k by a positive factor.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The FRW Christoffel symbol Gamma^theta_{phi phi} is printed as +sin theta cos theta in Exercise 13.14; it should be -sin theta cos theta.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign errors in geodesic or divergence calculations.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide a symbolic-algebra check of the connection coefficients.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The distance-redshift relations are given only to second order in z, while the chapter emphasizes z ~ 1 supernovae and z = 1090 CMB; the exact integral d_L = (1+z) R_0 S_k(integral of dz/(R_0 H(z))) with H(z) from the Friedmann equation is never written.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot reproduce Figure 13.3 curves or the CMB distance.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the exact comoving-distance integral and H(z) = H_0 sqrt(Omega_r(1+z)^4 + Omega_m(1+z)^3 + Omega_k(1+z)^2 + Omega_Lambda).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The age of the Universe is never computed for the Lambda-CDM parameters; only 1/H_0 (14 Gyr) and the matter-only 2/(3H_0) appear.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: No connection between Omega values and the familiar 13.8 Gyr.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Include the closed-form flat Lambda-CDM age formula and a numerical evaluation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The explanation of E and B modes treats polarization as an ordinary vector field and says about half of gravitational-wave polarization is divergence-free; real CMB polarization is a headless spin-2 field whose E/B split is defined by second derivatives, and the terminology 'divergence-free' versus 'curl-free' is used loosely.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Advanced learners may be confused when meeting the standard formalism.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the vector picture as a heuristic, then show headless sticks and the tangential/radial pattern around hot spots (E) versus swirling patterns (B).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text states that gravitational waves produce no temperature variations in the CMB. Tensor perturbations do generate large-angle temperature anisotropy (integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect along the photon path); what they cannot do is make E-only polarization, so B modes are the distinguishing signature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conclude tensor modes are invisible in temperature data, and then be confused by tensor-to-scalar ratio constraints that use temperature spectra.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say gravitational waves add no density perturbation at last scattering but do redshift photons anisotropically; show a TT spectrum with a tensor contribution confined to low l.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: String theory is said to require eleven spacetime dimensions; superstring theories are ten-dimensional and eleven dimensions belong to M-theory/supergravity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor factual slip in a survey passage.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State 10 for superstrings, 11 for M-theory.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The loss of photon energy is dismissed as 'just goes away' without explaining that cosmological spacetimes lack a timelike Killing vector, or showing the conformal Killing vector reasoning.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Leaves learners uneasy about energy conservation in GR.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Contrast Schwarzschild (static, conserved E) with FRW and discuss the local conservation law nabla_mu T^{mu nu} = 0 versus global energy.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The 'balloon' and embedding pictures, and the v > c objection, are not followed by a discussion of the Hubble sphere, event horizon, or superluminal recession; the text defers to Davis and Lineweaver.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Common confusions about galaxies receding faster than light persist.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add an interactive conformal diagram showing Hubble sphere, particle horizon and event horizon in Lambda-CDM.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chapter is a mid-2021 snapshot; later developments (LVK O4 results, JWST high-redshift galaxies, DESI BAO analyses hinting at evolving dark energy, updated H_0 measurements, Athena's re-scoping) are absent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Numbers and outlook will look dated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Keep the conceptual framework but attach a maintained 'current values' panel to observational sections.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The homogeneity derivation shows a constant curvature scalar is necessary but proves sufficiency only by checking the three cases; the statement that it is 'remarkably sufficient' in general is not proven and relies on isotropy about every point.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers may wonder whether other spaces with constant scalar curvature exist (they do, without isotropy).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Clarify that isotropy about every point plus constant curvature scalar implies maximal symmetry, and cite the Killing-vector argument.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book's account of how the CMB measures H_0 is physically muddled. The acoustic waves are said to travel in the dark matter. Photon drag is explained as compressional heating re-ionizing the gas. The Planck value is presented as coming from extrapolating today's BAO scale back to z = 1090. In fact the oscillations are sound waves in the tightly coupled photon-baryon fluid. The drag epoch is when Compton drag on baryons ends. Planck infers H_0 from the CMB alone, calibrating the acoustic angular scale with a sound horizon computed in Lambda-CDM.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners come away with a wrong picture of acoustic peaks and the drag epoch, and cannot see why the Hubble tension is model-dependent on the CMB side (the computed sound horizon is exactly what 'new early-Universe physics' proposals change).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach the sound horizon r_s = integral of c_s dt up to last scattering as the standard ruler and theta_* = r_s / D_M(z_*) as the measured angle. Present galaxy BAO as the same ruler seen at low redshift, and note that shrinking r_s would raise the CMB value of H_0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book says the singularity theorems prove our Universe certainly had a singularity whatever its asymmetry. The theorems establish geodesic incompleteness only under energy conditions. The one relevant here, the strong energy condition rho + 3p >= 0, is violated by the very dark energy and inflation the chapter goes on to use.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may think the Big Bang singularity is a theorem-level certainty of the actual Universe rather than a consequence of assumptions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Link the singularity argument to the acceleration equation. The same rho + 3p that decides deceleration also decides focusing, so an accelerating phase is exactly where the argument weakens.

tutor_notes: Open with a question: if the Universe is expanding, where is the centre? Use the balloon (with the embedding hidden) to show there is none, then ask what 'distance' could mean for a galaxy whose light left 10 billion years ago.

Order of explanation that works: observed facts (homogeneity, isotropy, v = Hd, CMB) -> cosmic time and comoving coordinates -> FRW metric and k -> redshift = expansion ratio -> operational distances -> only then Einstein's equations (Friedmann, acceleration) -> Omega budget -> thermal history.

Check understanding of redshift by asking the learner to predict wavelength of a photon emitted when the Universe was one-third its present size (z = 2) and whether that means the source moved at twice the speed of light (no).
When introducing the Friedmann equation, have the learner identify kinetic, potential and total-energy terms and predict the fate of a closed, matter-only universe before showing Figure 13.4.

For dark energy, ask: how can something with positive energy make expansion speed up? Guide toward rho + 3p and tension; then use Exercise 13.18 to kill the idea that tension 'pulls' the Universe outward or inward mechanically.

Distinguish carefully the particle horizon (causal, fundamental), the optical horizon (decoupling, not fundamental), and later the Hubble radius; learners conflate them. A spacetime diagram in conformal time helps.
Use the photon-counting derivation of d_L as a formative check: ask which factor of (1+z) comes from energy and which from arrival rate, and why d_A has (1+z)^{-2} relative to d_L.

When quoting numbers from 13.4, flag the known slips (Planck time formula, nucleosynthesis energy, equality epoch, decoupling redshift, e-fold count) and give modern values; encourage learners to recompute equality and decoupling from scaling laws.

Common learner question: 'Does space expand inside atoms or the Solar System?' Answer with the chapter's local-flatness point: bound systems are governed by local dynamics; the FRW expansion describes averages over scales above ~10 Mpc.

Common learner question: 'What came before the Big Bang?' Explain that classical GR cannot continue past R = 0, singularity theorems make this generic, but within a Planck time quantum gravity may change the story (loop cosmology bounces).
For the Hubble tension, have learners explain why supernovae measure d_L while the CMB and BAO measure d_A, and what each method assumes; avoid presenting either value as 'the right one'.

Link back to gravitational waves: ask why standard sirens need no distance ladder, why inclination matters (factor 4 in flux), and why primordial gravitational waves show up as B-mode polarization but not as temperature spots.
For learners with less mathematics, lean on the energy-budget bar chart and the balloon; for advanced learners, derive the Christoffel symbols (Exercise 13.14) and the exact d_L(z) integral.

When covering 'Using the CMB to measure H_0', do not repeat the book's mechanism. Explain acoustic peaks as sound waves in the photon-baryon fluid, the sound horizon as a ruler computed from early-Universe physics, and galaxy BAO as the same ruler seen later. Then ask why a smaller sound horizon would ease the Hubble tension.
